statement: A BSP starts with a 124-byte header: a signed 32-bit `version`, then 15 directory entries of a signed 32-bit `fileofs` and a signed 32-bit `filelen`, in the order of the lump table above.

`version` must be 29; any other value fails with the error `Mod_LoadBrushModel: <name> has wrong version number (<version> should be 29)` (fatal in id's engine). Because the loader is chosen by the magic of SPR-1.2 and MDL-1.2, any file that is not a sprite or an alias model is checked as a BSP.
Lump `n` is the `filelen` bytes at `fileofs`. Lumps may appear in the file in any order and need not be adjacent; the bytes between and after them are ignored.

Each lump of fixed-size elements (planes, vertexes, nodes, texinfo, faces, clipnodes, leafs, marksurfaces, edges, surfedges and models) must have a `filelen` that is a whole multiple of its element size; otherwise loading fails with the error `MOD_LoadBmodel: funny lump size in <name>` (fatal in id's engine). The element count is `filelen` divided by the element size, and an empty lump has none. The entities, textures, visibility and lighting lumps have no such check.

id's loader reads the lumps in this order, so of two faults the one in the earlier lump is reported: vertexes, edges, surfedges, textures, lighting, planes, texinfo, faces, marksurfaces, visibility, leafs, nodes, clipnodes, entities, models.

A file shorter than the header, or a lump whose `fileofs` or `filelen` is negative or whose bytes run past the end of the file, fails to load. id's code reads the header and lumps from the loaded buffer without checking them, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

**Withdrawn** 2026-10-16: it made every visibility offset name a byte of the lump, but `qbsp` gives leaf 0 the offset 0 even when the visibility lump is empty, which id's loader never reads; replaced by BSP-1.8 and BSP-6.6.

An index stored in one lump that refers to another (a plane, texinfo, edge, surfedge, face, node, leaf, clipnode or vertex number, or an offset into the visibility or lighting lump) must name an element that exists; one that does not fails to load, except for the visibility offsets of BSP-6.6. An index is checked where the loader uses it: an edge's vertices and a surfedge's edge when a face uses them, and a model's first node or clipnode for hulls 0 to 2, since hull 3 is not used (BSP-11.3). id's code checks only the cases BSP-8.3 and BSP-13.2 name and uses every other index unchecked, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
The entities lump is text: a sequence of entities, each `{`, then `"key" "value"` pairs, then `}`, tokenised by `COM_Parse` and applied by EDICT-8.

The text ends at its first NUL byte or at the end of the lump, whichever comes first. id's engine copies exactly `filelen` bytes and parses until a NUL; id's `qbsp` writes a NUL after the text and counts it in `filelen` (`qutils/QBSP/MAP.C`, `WriteEntitiesToString`: `entdatasize = end - buf + 1`), so a lump without one is read past its end, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as the end of the lump.
An empty entities lump loads; the map then has no entities.
The first entity is the world (EDICT-4); a brush entity names its model with a `model` key of the form `*<n>` (BSP-15.3).
A plane is the 20-byte `dplane_t`: the set of points `p` with `dot(normal, p) = dist`. Its front is the side `normal` points to.

`type` is 0, 1 or 2 (`PLANE_X`, `PLANE_Y`, `PLANE_Z`) for a plane whose normal is along that axis, and 3, 4 or 5 (`PLANE_ANYX` to `PLANE_ANYZ`) for one whose normal is closest to that axis. The loader copies `type` without checking it or the normal, so any value loads.
On load each plane gets `signbits`: bit `j` is set when `normal[j] < 0`. `-0.0` is not less than 0, so it sets no bit.
An empty textures lump loads with no textures; every texinfo then uses the engine's checkerboard texture with flags 0 (BSP-8.4).

Otherwise the lump starts with a signed 32-bit `nummiptex` and `nummiptex` signed 32-bit offsets, each from the start of the lump. An offset of -1 is a missing texture: that slot is empty and a texinfo naming it uses the checkerboard (BSP-8.4).

At each other offset is a 40-byte `miptex_t`: a 16-byte name, a 32-bit `width` and `height`, and four 32-bit offsets from the start of the `miptex_t`. The name is the bytes before the first NUL, or all 16.
`width` and `height` must each be a multiple of 16; otherwise loading fails with the error `Texture <name> is not 16 aligned` (fatal in id's engine).

The engine copies `width * height / 64 * 85` bytes from right after the 40-byte header, the four mip levels of `width * height`, a quarter, a sixteenth and a sixty-fourth of that, and finds each level at its `offsets[j]`. A texture whose levels do not lie in those bytes, or whose bytes run past the lump, fails to load: id's code copies them unchecked, which is undefined, and this spec fixes the answer as an error. `qbsp` writes the levels in order right after the header (offsets 40, `40 + w*h`, and so on).
A negative `nummiptex`, or one whose offset table runs past the lump, fails to load, as does an offset other than -1 that points outside the lump (BSP-1.8).
A texture whose name starts with `sky` (compared exactly, case included) is a sky: the loader hands it to the renderer's `R_InitSky`.

A texture whose name starts with `+` is a frame of an animation. The second character, upper-cased if it is a letter, is `0` to `9` for frame 0 to 9 of the primary animation, or `A` to `J` for frame 0 to 9 of the alternate animation; anything else fails with the error `Bad animating texture <name>` (fatal in id's engine). Frames belong to the same animation when their names match from the third character on, case included.

An animation of `n` primary frames needs every frame from 0 to `n - 1`, where `n` is one more than the highest frame present, and likewise for the alternate frames; a gap fails with the error `Missing frame <i> of <name>`, where `<name>` is the first texture of that animation in lump order (fatal in id's engine). Each frame's next frame is the following one, wrapping to frame 0; each frame lasts `ANIM_CYCLE` (2) units of the animation's total of `2 * n`. When an animation has both kinds, every primary frame's alternate is alternate frame 0 and every alternate frame's alternate is primary frame 0.
When two textures claim the same frame of one animation, the later one in lump order takes the frame and the earlier one is not part of the cycle.
A vertex is 12 bytes: three floats, x, y and z, in map units.
The visibility lump is raw bytes. A leaf's `visofs` (BSP-12.1) is the offset of its set in the lump, or -1 for none.
A set decompresses to a row of `(visleafs + 7) >> 3` bytes, where `visleafs` is model 0's `visleafs` (BSP-15.1). Bit `k` of the row (byte `k >> 3`, bit `k & 7`) is leaf `k + 1`: leaf 0 has no bit.

Decompression reads a byte: if it is not 0 it is copied to the row; if it is 0 the next byte is a count and that many 0 bytes are written. It stops as soon as the row is full, checked after each copied byte or run, so a run may end past the row; only the row's bytes count. A run of count 0 writes nothing.
Leaf 0, and any leaf whose `visofs` is -1, sees every leaf: its row is all `0xFF`.

A set whose compressed bytes run past the end of the lump before the row is full fails to decompress. id's code reads past the lump, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error for that leaf's set.

Leaf 0's `visofs` is never read (BSP-6.4), so any value loads. When the visibility lump is empty, `Mod_LoadVisibility` keeps no data (`loadmodel->visdata = NULL`) and `Mod_LoadLeafs` sets a leaf's set to `loadmodel->visdata + p`, so a `visofs` of 0 gives no set, which `Mod_DecompressVis` reads as every leaf visible, as -1 does. Any other `visofs` but -1 into an empty lump fails to load (BSP-1.8). `qbsp`'s `BeginBSPFile` sets only leaf 0's `contents` in its zeroed leaf array, so leaf 0's `visofs` is 0, also in a BSP that `vis` has not processed.

A row's width follows model 0's `visleafs` alone, not the number of leaves the file holds: id's `Mod_DecompressVis` has `row = (model->numleafs+7)>>3;` and `Mod_LoadBrushModel` sets `mod->numleafs = bm->visleafs;`, and QS does the same, growing its buffer to the row (`mod_decompressed = (byte *) realloc (mod_decompressed, mod_decompressed_capacity);`). So a file of a few hundred bytes can make every row, and the all-visible row of BSP-6.4 that reads no input, as wide as `visleafs` says. `visleafs` is a signed 32-bit count, so a row is at most `BSP_MAX_VIS_ROW` bytes, the bound on what one leaf's set costs; id's `numleafs+7` overflows `int` for the seven largest counts, which is undefined in C, and this spec fixes the answer as `BSP_MAX_VIS_ROW`. A `visleafs` of -7 to -1 gives a row of 0 bytes; one of -8 or less makes `row` negative, for which id's all-visible loop `while (row)` does not end, and this spec fixes the answer as a row of 0 bytes too. id's buffer holds `MAX_MAP_LEAFS/8` bytes, so in id's code a row wider than that is undefined (BSP-20.18); this spec follows QS for every loader.
A node is the 24-byte `dnode_t`. It splits space by plane `planenum`: `children[0]` is the front and `children[1]` the back.
A child `c` of 0 or more is node `c`; a negative child is leaf `-1 - c`, so -1 is leaf 0.
`mins` and `maxs` are the node's bounding box in whole map units, for culling.
`firstface` and `numfaces` are the faces (BSP-9) that lie on the node's plane, read as unsigned 16-bit values.

The nodes of the drawing hull are also collision hull 0: each node becomes a clipnode with the same plane, a child node keeping its number and a child leaf replaced by that leaf's `contents` (BSP-12.2).
A BSP with no nodes fails to load. id's code reads node 0 regardless (`Mod_SetParent`), which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
A texinfo is the 40-byte `texinfo_t`. A point `p` on a face using it has the texture coordinates `s = dot(vecs[0].xyz, p) + vecs[0][3]` and `t = dot(vecs[1].xyz, p) + vecs[1][3]`, in texels.
`miptex` is an index into the textures lump's slots (BSP-4.2).

When the textures lump is not empty, a `miptex` of `nummiptex` or more fails with the error `miptex >= loadmodel->numtextures` (fatal in id's engine). A negative `miptex` is not checked and indexes before the array, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
When the textures lump is empty, or the slot is a missing texture, the texinfo uses the engine's checkerboard texture and its flags become 0, whatever the file says.

`flags` bit 0 (`TEX_SPECIAL`, 1) marks a texture with no lightmap and no size limit: sky and liquids. `qbsp` sets it for textures whose names start with `*` or with `sky` in any case (MAP-4.5). Other bits are kept and not interpreted.

On load each texinfo gets a mip bias from the mean length `m` of its two axes: 4 when `m < 0.32`, 3 when `m < 0.49`, 2 when `m < 0.99`, otherwise 1. The lengths and their mean are single-precision floats, compared with the constants as doubles.
A face is the 20-byte `dface_t`: a convex polygon on plane `planenum`, facing the plane's front when `side` is 0 and its back for any other value.
The face's vertices are the `numedges` surfedges from `firstedge` (BSP-14.2), in order.

**Withdrawn** 2026-10-16: it said the texture coordinates are computed in single precision, but id's original x86 builds compute them on the x87 with exact products and one rounding to single precision, which gives 247 faces of LibreQuake's maps another `texturemins` or extent; replaced by BSP-9.10, BSP-9.11 and BSP-9.12.
When the texinfo's flags (after BSP-8.4) do not have `TEX_SPECIAL`, an extent over 256 fails with the error `Bad surface extents` (fatal in id's engine); 256 loads.

A face whose texture name starts with `sky` is drawn as sky; one whose name starts with `*` is a liquid, drawn warped, and its extents become 16384 and its `texturemins` -8192 after the check of BSP-9.4.
`styles` are up to four light styles; the first 255 ends the list. `lightofs` is -1 for a face with no light samples, otherwise the offset of its samples in the lighting lump.

A face's lightmap is `smax = (extents[0] >> 4) + 1` samples wide and `tmax = (extents[1] >> 4) + 1` high, one sample per 16 texels, stored row by row; there is one lightmap of `smax * tmax` samples for each style before the first 255, one after another from `lightofs`.
`planenum`, `numedges` and `texinfo` are signed 16-bit and `firstedge` signed 32-bit; a negative value, or one that names no element, fails to load (BSP-1.8).

**Withdrawn** 2026-10-16: it said the products and the difference that follow the conversion wrap as 32-bit x86 integers and that such a face fails BSP-9.4 unless its texinfo has `TEX_SPECIAL`, but id's loader stores `texturemins` and `extents` in 16-bit fields and checks the stored value, so an extent of 65536 + 16 loads, and a face whose bounds both convert to the indefinite value has extent 0 and loads; replaced by BSP-9.13 and BSP-9.14.

The face's texture extents are computed from its vertices' texture coordinates (BSP-8.1, BSP-9.11). For each axis the running minimum starts at 999999 and the maximum at -99999, and each vertex's coordinate in turn may replace them (BSP-9.12); then `bmin = floor(min / 16)` and `bmax = ceil(max / 16)`, `texturemins = bmin * 16` and `extents = (bmax - bmin) * 16`.

A vertex `(x, y, z)`'s texture coordinate on an axis `(s0, s1, s2, offset)` is computed as id's x86 builds of WinQuake and GLQuake compute it: the three products, each exact, are added in the order `((x * s0 + z * s2) + y * s1) + offset`, each sum rounded to 53 bits (double precision, round to nearest even), and the result is rounded once to single precision. It is not single-precision arithmetic, and the order is not C's. Once WinQuake has drawn a frame it adds at 64 bits instead, and id's DOS and Linux builds add in C's order (see the evidence below); these answers differ only when a sum lies so close to a midpoint of two singles that the order or the precision of the additions decides how it rounds (vectors `x87-order` and `x87-pc64`), which no face of LibreQuake's maps does. This spec takes 53 bits, the precision GLQuake always uses.

A coordinate replaces the running minimum unless it is greater than or equal to it, and the running maximum unless the maximum is greater than or equal to it, as WinQuake's and GLQuake's x86 code compares: a NaN coordinate replaces both, and the next coordinate replaces a NaN minimum or maximum. A bound that is still NaN after the last vertex gives the integer indefinite value of BSP-9.13.

`CalcSurfaceExtents` stores `floor(min / 16)` and `ceil(max / 16)` in `int` variables, which is undefined in C when the value is NaN or outside the `int` range. This spec takes the answer of the original x86 build, whose conversion gives the integer indefinite value 0x80000000 (-2147483648) there; BSP-9.14 then keeps the low 16 bits of what BSP-9.10 computes from it.

`texturemins` and `extents` are `short` fields of `msurface_t` (`WinQuake/model.h` and `WinQuake/gl_model.h`: `short texturemins[2];` and `short extents[2];`), so `CalcSurfaceExtents` stores the low 16 bits of each value BSP-9.10 computes, read as a signed two's-complement value: a value from -32768 to 32767 is kept, an extent of 65552 is stored as 16 and one of 32784 as -32752, and a `texturemins` of 32768 as -32768. The check of BSP-9.4 and the lightmap size of BSP-9.7 use the stored value, so a stored extent of 256 or less, negative ones included, passes BSP-9.4. The conversion to `short` is implementation-defined in C; this spec takes the answer of id's x86 builds, which compute, store and compare the 16-bit value (see the evidence below).
**Withdrawn** 2026-10-16: it said `crates/qs-bsp` has no default loader, but ADR-0012 made the FitzQuake lineage's the default; replaced by BSP-9.17.

A face whose stored extent (BSP-9.14) is negative on either axis has no lightmap: this spec gives it 0 by 0 samples, so it has no samples and BSP-10.2 requires only that its `lightofs` is -1 or at most the size of the lighting lump. BSP-9.7 would give that axis `(extent >> 4) + 1` samples, 0 or fewer (id's x86 builds shift the `short` arithmetically), and neither of id's renderers draws light from the face's samples: WinQuake stops with `D_SCAlloc: bad cache width` or `D_SCAlloc: bad cache size` the first time it caches the face to draw it, before it reads a sample; GLQuake stops with `AllocBlock: full` when a map starts if `smax` is below 0 and `tmax` above 0, and otherwise stores none of the face's samples in its lightmap texture; and neither lights a model from the face. id's loaders load the face (BSP-9.14); what each renderer does is in the evidence below.

GLQuake's `CalcSurfaceExtents` (`WinQuake/gl_model.c`) checks `s->extents[i] > 512 /* 256 */` where WinQuake's checks `s->extents[i] > 256` (BSP-9.4): when the texinfo's flags do not have `TEX_SPECIAL`, a stored extent (BSP-9.14) over 512 fails with `Bad surface extents` and 512 loads, so a face with an extent from 272 to 512 loads in GLQuake and fails in WinQuake. `crates/qs-bsp` applies the limit of the loader its caller names: 256 for `BspLoader::WinQuake`, 512 for `BspLoader::GlQuake`, and 2000 for `BspLoader::FitzQuake`, the default (BSP-20.10).
The lighting lump is one unsigned byte per lightmap sample, 0 darkest; faces index it by `lightofs` (BSP-9.6, BSP-9.7). An empty lump means the map has no light data and is drawn fully bright.
A face's samples (`smax * tmax` times its number of styles from `lightofs`) must lie in the lump; otherwise it fails to load (BSP-1.8).
A clipnode is the 8-byte `dclipnode_t`: plane `planenum` and a front and back child. A child of 0 or more is that clipnode; a negative child is a contents value (BSP-12.2) ending the walk.
The clipnodes lump holds collision hulls 1 and 2 of every model; a model's `headnode[1]` and `headnode[2]` (BSP-15.1) are their first clipnodes. Hull 0 is the nodes (BSP-7.5).

Hull 1 is the hull for an entity of size (-16, -16, -24) to (16, 16, 32), the player, and hull 2 for (-32, -32, -24) to (32, 32, 64). A `SOLID_BSP` entity is collided with hull 0 when the other entity's x size is under 3, hull 1 when it is at most 32, and hull 2 otherwise. Hull 3 is not used.

A leaf is the 28-byte `dleaf_t`: a convex region of space with one contents value, its visibility offset (BSP-6.1), its bounding box in whole map units, the range of marksurfaces (BSP-13) listing the faces that can be seen in it, and four ambient sound levels.
`contents` is one of the `CONTENTS_` values: -1 empty, -2 solid, -3 water, -4 slime, -5 lava, -6 sky. The loader copies it without checking.

Leaf 0 is the shared solid leaf that every solid region points to; `qbsp` gives it `CONTENTS_SOLID` and no faces (`qutils/QBSP/WRITEBSP.C`, `BeginBSPFile`: "leaf 0 is common solid with no faces"), and it has no visibility bit (BSP-6.2).
`ambient_level` is the volume, 0 to 255, of the water, sky, slime and lava ambient sounds, in that order.

`firstmarksurface` and `nummarksurfaces` are read as unsigned 16-bit values. id's loader reads them through `LittleShort`, which returns a signed `short`, so a value of 32768 or more indexes before the array, which is undefined; this spec reads them as the file declares them, as QS does.

GLQuake's `Mod_LoadLeafs` (`WinQuake/gl_model.c`) sets `SURF_UNDERWATER` (0x80, `WinQuake/gl_model.h`) in the flags of every face that a leaf whose `contents` is not -1 (`CONTENTS_EMPTY`) lists among its marksurfaces (BSP-13.1), whatever the face's texture and other flags: a face listed by a water, slime, lava, sky or solid leaf, or by a leaf whose value is no `CONTENTS_` value, has it, and keeps it when an empty leaf lists it too. WinQuake's `Mod_LoadLeafs` (`WinQuake/model.c`) has no such code and `WinQuake/model.h` defines no such flag, so no face WinQuake loads has 0x80. `crates/qs-bsp` sets the flag when its caller names GLQuake's loader (BSP-9.17), over the marksurfaces BSP-12.5 reads and for BSP2 as for BSP29, and never when it names WinQuake's.

id's loaders tell a leaf from a node by its `contents` alone: `Mod_SetParent` has `if (node->contents < 0)` `return;` and `Mod_MakeHull0` has `if (child->contents < 0)` `out->children[j] = child->contents;` `else` `out->children[j] = child - loadmodel->nodes;`, in `WinQuake/model.c` and `WinQuake/gl_model.c` alike. A leaf whose `contents` is 0 or more is copied without a check (BSP-12.2), and a node that names it hands it to those functions as a node. When node 0's tree reaches it, `Mod_SetParent` (called from `Mod_LoadNodes` with `Mod_SetParent (loadmodel->nodes, NULL);`) reads the leaf's `efrags`, which `Mod_LoadLeafs` sets to `NULL`, as the node's first child and writes through it: both loaders crash. When only another model's nodes name it, the load completes and `Mod_MakeHull0` gives that hull 0 child the distance between the leaf and the node array, a subtraction of pointers into two arrays that C leaves undefined. A leaf no node names loads with its contents. `crates/qs-bsp` fails a BSP in which any node names a leaf whose contents is 0 or more, with every loader (`BspError::LeafContents`), and loads one whose only such leaves no node names.
The marksurfaces lump is a list of 16-bit face numbers, read as unsigned (as BSP-12.5); a leaf's faces are its `nummarksurfaces` entries from `firstmarksurface`.
A face number that is not below the number of faces fails with the error `Mod_ParseMarksurfaces: bad surface number` (fatal in id's engine).
An edge is 4 bytes: two unsigned 16-bit vertex numbers, `v[0]` and `v[1]`. Edge 0 is never used, because its number cannot be negated; `qbsp` writes it as a placeholder.

A surfedge is a signed 32-bit edge number. A value `e` of 0 or more uses edge `e` from `v[0]` to `v[1]`, so the face's vertex is `v[0]`; a negative value uses edge `-e` backwards, so the vertex is its `v[1]`.
A surfedge of -2147483648 has no positive counterpart and fails to load. id's code negates it, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

A model is the 64-byte `dmodel_t`: its bounds, an origin, the first node of hull 0 and first clipnode of hulls 1 to 3 in `headnode`, the number of leaves with visibility (not counting leaf 0), and the range of faces drawn for it.
Model 0 is the world. Its `visleafs` sets the width of every visibility row (BSP-6.2).
Model `n` above 0 is the brush model named `*<n>`, which a brush entity uses through its `model` key. The server precaches the world as model 1 and `*<n>` as model `n + 1`.

On load each model's `mins` are lowered and `maxs` raised by 1 on every axis, and its radius is the length of the vector whose components are the larger absolute value of `mins[j]` and `maxs[j]`, after that change.
`origin` is read and not used by id's engine.
A BSP with no models fails to load. id's loader then leaves the world without bounds or hull heads; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
The `MAX_MAP_` limits below are the sizes of `qbsp`'s and the other tools' arrays; id's engine checks none of them when it loads a BSP.

A BSP29 file cannot refer past what its fields hold: a node child names node 0 to 32767 or leaf 0 to 32767 (BSP-7.2), a clipnode child names clipnode 0 to 32767 (BSP-11.1), an edge names vertex 0 to 65535 (BSP-14.1), a face names plane and texinfo 0 to 32767 (BSP-9.8), and a node's faces and a marksurface name face 0 to 65535 (BSP-7.4, BSP-13.1).

A `2PSB` file's version field is the bytes `2PSB` (0x32 0x50 0x53 0x42, the 32-bit value 0x42535032) and a `BSP2` file's is the bytes `BSP2` (0x42 0x53 0x50 0x32, the value 0x32505342). The header and directory are otherwise those of BSP-1.1.

The entities, planes, textures, vertexes, visibility, texinfo, lighting, surfedges and models lumps are those of BSP29; the other six use the structures in the table above, with the same fields in the same order, widened.
In both variants a node child or clipnode child is a signed 32-bit value read as BSP-7.2 and BSP-11.1, and edge vertex numbers, marksurface entries and a leaf's marksurface range are unsigned 32-bit.
A `2PSB` node or leaf keeps 16-bit integer bounds; a `BSP2` node or leaf has float bounds, `mins[3]` then `maxs[3]`.
**Withdrawn** 2026-10-16: it applied BSP-1 to BSP-15 to BSP2 whatever the loader, but the FitzQuake lineage's loader, the default, reads BSP2 by BSP-20; replaced by BSP-17.6.

id's WinQuake and GLQuake read no BSP2 (BSP-1.2); `crates/qs-bsp` reads it with every loader. With `BspLoader::WinQuake` or `BspLoader::GlQuake`, every rule of BSP-1 to BSP-15 that does not concern a field's width applies to BSP2 unchanged. With `BspLoader::FitzQuake`, the default, BSP2 is read as QS reads it: those rules as BSP-20 changes them, BSP-20.16 for node children and no limit on leaves (BSP-20.13).

A `.lit` file is the 4 bytes `QLIT`, a signed 32-bit version 1, and then 3 bytes, red, green and blue, for each byte of the BSP's lighting lump, in the same order, so `lightofs` (BSP-9.6) indexes it after multiplying by 3.

QS uses a `.lit` only when its size is exactly `8 + 3 * filelen` of the BSP's lighting lump; otherwise it prints `Outdated .lit file (<name> should be <n> bytes, not <m>)` and uses the BSP's own light.

A file that does not start with `QLIT` is ignored (`Corrupt .lit file (old version?), ignoring`), and one with another version is ignored (`Unknown .lit file version (<version>)`). ericw-tools also writes a version 0x00010001 holding one packed 32-bit `E5BGR9` HDR sample per lighting byte; QS does not read it, and this spec does not describe it further.
QS ignores a `.lit` found in a game directory of lower priority than the BSP (`ignored <name> from a gamedir with lower priority`), so a mod's BSP never takes the base game's `.lit`.
Without a usable `.lit`, each lighting byte stands for the grey triple of that value.

Only the FitzQuake lineage's loader reads a `.lit` (QS's `Mod_LoadLighting`, called from `Mod_LoadBrushModel`); id's WinQuake and GLQuake `Mod_LoadLighting` copy the lighting lump alone, so a map loaded by their rules is lit grey. `crates/qs-bsp` reads a `.lit` with `Lit::read`, apart from `Bsp::read`, whichever loader read the BSP; the caller decides whether it applies, as it does for a map the default loader read.

QS checks a `.lit` it finds in this order and stops at the first check that fails: the game directory's priority (BSP-18.4), the magic, the version (BSP-18.3), then the size (BSP-18.2). `Mod_LoadLighting` reads `if (path_id < loadmodel->path_id)` first, then `else if (data[0] == 'Q' && data[1] == 'L' && data[2] == 'I' && data[3] == 'T')`, `if (i == 1)` and `if (8+l->filelen*3 == com_filesize)`. So a `.lit` from a game directory of lower priority is ignored whatever it holds, and its message is printed with `Con_DPrintf`, which prints nothing unless the `developer` cvar is set (`if (!developer.value) return;`); the messages of BSP-18.2 and BSP-18.3 are printed with `Con_Printf`, always.

A `.lit` QS ignores never stops the map loading. Each branch of BSP-18.7 that ignores the file frees it (`Hunk_FreeToLowMark(mark);`), prints its message and falls through to `// LordHavoc: no .lit found, expand the white lighting data to color`, the grey light of BSP-18.5; only the size check that passes returns early, after `loadmodel->lightdata = data + 8;`. `crates/qs-bsp`'s `mod_load_lighting` makes this choice for a map: the `.lit` used, or why it is ignored with QS's message, and never an error. For `BspLoader::WinQuake` and `BspLoader::GlQuake` it reads no `.lit` (BSP-18.6).

When its `external_ents` cvar is set (its default is `"1"`), QS looks for the entity text in `<map>@<crc>.ent` and then in `<map>.ent`, where `<map>` is the BSP's name with its extension removed by `COM_StripExtension` (the last `.` after the last `/` or `\`, and not the name's first byte), and uses the first it finds instead of the entity lump. `<crc>` is `CRC_Block` (the CRC of PROGS-4) of the lump's first `filelen - 1` bytes, which leaves out the NUL `qbsp` writes (BSP-2.2), formatted with `%04x`; it is 0 for an empty lump.
QS ignores a `.ent` file found in a game directory of lower priority than the BSP's (`ignored <name> from a gamedir with lower priority`), as it does a `.lit` (BSP-18.4).

This project writes edited entities in either place. A BSP is rewritten with the new text and a NUL as its entity lump and every other lump's bytes unchanged, the lumps in the order of their offsets in the original file, each at an offset that is a multiple of 4; a `.ent` file is the text alone.

`BspLoader::FitzQuake` is the default loader. It loads a BSP by BSP-1 to BSP-17 except where BSP-20.2 to BSP-20.17 say otherwise. Where QS, like id, uses an index or offset from the file without checking it (a plane, texinfo, edge, vertex, face or marksurface range, a visibility or lighting offset, a texture's header), the answer this spec fixes for id's loaders holds (BSP-1.6, BSP-1.8, BSP-4.6, BSP-6.5, BSP-10.2, BSP-14.3). `BspLoader::WinQuake` and `BspLoader::GlQuake` are unchanged.

QS's `Mod_LoadBrushModel` also accepts version 30 (`case BSPVERSION_VALVE:`, Half-Life's format, compiled in because `Quake/quakedef.h` has `#define BSP29_VALVE // enable Half-Life map support`) and `Q64 ` (`case BSPVERSION_QUAKE64:`, Quake 64's), and fails any other with `Mod_LoadBrushModel: %s has unsupported version number (%i)`. `qs-bsp` reads neither format with any loader and fails both, and every other version that is not BSP29 or BSP2, with BSP-1.2's error: the plan requirement MAP-6 (`plan/requirements.yaml`) asks for Quake's formats only. The vector `version-30` loads in QS and fails in `qs-bsp`, a difference the differential run expects.

A texture whose width or height is 0 leaves its slot empty: `if (mt->width == 0 || mt->height == 0)` then `Con_Warning ("Zero sized texture %s in %s!\n", mt->name, loadmodel->name);` and `continue;`, so a texinfo naming it has a missing texture (BSP-20.7). GLQuake loads it, with no pixels. `qs-bsp` leaves the slot `None`.

A texture whose width or height is not a multiple of 16 loads: `Con_Warning ("Texture %s (%d x %d) is not 16 aligned\n", mt->name, mt->width, mt->height);` where GLQuake has `Sys_Error ("Texture %s is not 16 aligned", mt->name);` (BSP-4.4).

QS copies only mip level 0, `pixels = mt->width*mt->height; // only copy the first mip, the rest are auto-generated`, from right after the 40-byte header, and never reads `offsets` except to see whether `offsets[0]` is 0 (`// an offset of zero indicates an external texture`, which QS looks up in the WADs the world's `wad` key names when its `external_textures` cvar is set, and reads from the BSP when none has it). Bytes past the end of the lump are not copied (`if (((byte*)(mt+1) + lump_bytes) > (mod_base + l->fileofs + l->filelen))`, then `Con_DPrintf("Texture %s extends past end of lump\n", mt->name);` and the count cut to what is left), so level 0 may be short or empty. GLQuake copies `mt->width*mt->height/64*85` bytes unchecked (BSP-4.5). `qs-bsp` keeps level 0's `width * height` bytes, cut at the end of the lump, as `Texture::pixels`, and reads only the BSP. `width * height` is a C `unsigned` product stored in an `int`; one over 2^31 - 1 would make QS copy a negative count, and this spec fixes the answer as an error.

A texture is a sky when its name starts with `sky` in any case: `if (!q_strncasecmp(tx->name,"sky",3)) //sky texture //also note -- was Q_strncmp, changed to match qbsp` in `Mod_LoadTextures` and the same test in `Mod_LoadFaces`, where GLQuake has `if (!Q_strncmp(mt->name,"sky",3))` (BSP-4.7, BSP-9.5). `q_strncasecmp` folds only ASCII `A` to `Z`. `qs-bsp` sets `Texture::sky` and the face flags of BSP-20.11 by this test.

`Mod_LoadTexinfo` never fails on `miptex`. QS allocates `loadmodel->numtextures = nummiptex + 2` slots, the last two the checkerboard textures `r_notexture_mip` and `r_notexture_mip2`, and has `if (miptex >= loadmodel->numtextures-1 || !loadmodel->textures[miptex])` then the checkerboard (`r_notexture_mip2` with `TEX_SPECIAL`, otherwise `r_notexture_mip`) and `out->flags |= TEX_MISSING;` (`#define TEX_MISSING 2 // johnfitz -- this texinfo does not have a texture`), keeping the file's flags. So a `miptex` greater than `nummiptex`, or naming an empty slot, is missing; a `miptex` equal to `nummiptex` names `r_notexture_mip` itself and is not; with an empty textures lump `nummiptex` is 0. GLQuake fails a `miptex` of `nummiptex` or more (BSP-8.3) and zeroes the flags of a missing texture (BSP-8.4). A negative `miptex` indexes before the array, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as BSP-8.3's error. QS's `mtexinfo_t` has no mip bias; `qs-bsp` still gives BSP-8.6's.

`CalcSurfaceExtents` starts the bounds at `mins[0] = mins[1] = FLT_MAX;` and `maxs[0] = maxs[1] = -FLT_MAX;` where GLQuake starts them at 999999 and -99999 (BSP-9.10), and compares in C, `if (val < mins[j])` and `if (val > maxs[j])`, so a NaN coordinate replaces neither (against BSP-9.12). A bound no coordinate replaced, as in a face with no edges, stays `FLT_MAX` or `-FLT_MAX`, and `floor` or `ceil` of it divided by 16 is out of the `int` range; this spec takes the answer of the x86-64 build, whose conversion gives 0x80000000 as in BSP-9.13 (an arm64 build saturates instead and gives another answer). BSP-9.14 holds: QS's `msurface_t` has `short texturemins[2];` and `short extents[2];`.

Each texture coordinate is computed in double precision in C's order, `val = ((double)v->position[0] * (double)tex->vecs[j][0]) + ((double)v->position[1] * (double)tex->vecs[j][1]) + ((double)v->position[2] * (double)tex->vecs[j][2]) + (double)tex->vecs[j][3];`, and rounded once to single precision when stored in `float val`; QS's comment above it says the calculation "needs to produce the same result that the light compiler does". GLQuake writes the same sum in `float`, which id's x86 build evaluates as BSP-9.11 says. The products are exact in both; the answers differ only when the order of the additions decides a rounding (vector `x87-order`). `qs-bsp` computes the double sum in C's order.

The limit on extents is 2000: `if ( !(tex->flags & TEX_SPECIAL) && s->extents[i] > 2000) //johnfitz -- was 512 in glquake, 256 in winquake`, where GLQuake has `s->extents[i] > 512 /* 256 */` (BSP-9.17). Extents are multiples of 16, so 1984 is the largest that loads without `TEX_SPECIAL` and 2016 the smallest that fails.

`Mod_LoadFaces` sets these flags by the texture's name, the first that applies, where GLQuake sets only the sky and liquid flags of BSP-9.5: a name starting with `sky` in any case (BSP-20.6) gets `SURF_DRAWSKY | SURF_DRAWTILED`; one starting with `*` or `!` (`else if (out->texinfo->texture->name[0] == '*' || out->texinfo->texture->name[0] == '!') // warp surface`) gets `SURF_DRAWTURB`, `SURF_DRAWTILED` only when the texinfo has `TEX_SPECIAL` (`if (out->texinfo->flags & TEX_SPECIAL)`), and `SURF_DRAWLAVA`, `SURF_DRAWSLIME` or `SURF_DRAWTELE` when the name starts, case included (`strncmp`), with `*lava` or `!lava`, `*slime` or `!slime`, `*tele` or `!tele`, otherwise `SURF_DRAWWATER`; its extents and `texturemins` stay as BSP-20.8 computes them, where GLQuake sets 16384 and -8192, so a liquid without `TEX_SPECIAL` keeps its lightmap (`Con_DPrintf ("Map has lit water\n")`) and BSP-10.2 applies to it; a name starting with `{` (`// ericw -- fence textures`) gets `SURF_DRAWFENCE`; otherwise a face whose texinfo's flags have `TEX_MISSING` (set by BSP-20.7 or stored in the file) gets `SURF_NOTEXTURE`, and `SURF_DRAWTILED` too when its `lightofs` is -1. The values are QS's `Quake/gl_model.h`: `SURF_NOTEXTURE` 0x100, `SURF_DRAWFENCE` 0x200, `SURF_DRAWLAVA` 0x400, `SURF_DRAWSLIME` 0x800, `SURF_DRAWTELE` 0x1000, `SURF_DRAWWATER` 0x2000; `SURF_PLANEBACK` (BSP-9.1) is set as before.

No face gets `SURF_UNDERWATER`: each of QS's `Mod_ProcessLeafs_S`, `_L1` and `_L2` ends with `//johnfitz -- removed code to mark surfaces as SURF_UNDERWATER`, where GLQuake's `Mod_LoadLeafs` sets it (BSP-12.6).

A BSP29 file with more than 32767 leaves fails: `if (count > 32767)` then `Host_Error ("Mod_LoadLeafs: %i leafs exceeds limit of 32767.", count);` in `Mod_ProcessLeafs_S`, after the lump-size check. GLQuake has no limit, and neither have QS's BSP2 readers. `qs-bsp` gives `BspError::TooManyLeafs` with that message.

A BSP29 leaf's marksurface range and the marksurfaces lump are read as unsigned 16-bit values (`out->firstmarksurface = loadmodel->marksurfaces + (unsigned short)LittleShort(in->firstmarksurface); //johnfitz -- unsigned short`, and `j = (unsigned short)LittleShort(in[i]); //johnfitz -- explicit cast as unsigned short` in `Mod_LoadMarksurfaces`), where GLQuake's `LittleShort` gives a signed value. BSP-12.5 and BSP-13.1 already read them unsigned for every loader, so the loaders agree.

A BSP29 node child is read unsigned and is a node when it is below the node count, otherwise leaf 65535 minus it, and leaf 0 when that leaf does not exist: `p = (unsigned short)LittleShort(in->children[j]);`, `if (p < count)` a node, else `p = 65535 - p; //note this uses 65535 intentionally, -1 is leaf 0` and `if (p < loadmodel->numleafs)` that leaf, else `Con_Printf("Mod_LoadNodes: invalid leaf index %i (file has only %i leafs)\n", p, loadmodel->numleafs);` and `out->children[j] = (mnode_t *)(loadmodel->leafs); //map it to the solid leaf`. So a map of more than 32768 nodes can name nodes above 32767, which GLQuake reads as leaves (BSP-7.2, BSP-16.2). GLQuake uses a leaf that does not exist unchecked, and this spec fails it (BSP-1.8). `qs-bsp` writes the child it reads as BSP-7.2 does, node `n` as `n` and leaf `l` as `-1 - l`, so `Bsp::hull0` follows it.

A BSP2 node child is a node when it is below the node count and at least 0 (`2PSB`, `if (p >= 0 && p < count)`) or at least 1 (`BSP2`, `if (p > 0 && p < count)`), otherwise leaf `-1 - child`, computed as `p = 0xffffffff - p;`, and leaf 0 when that leaf does not exist, with the message of BSP-20.15. So a `BSP2` child of 0 is leaf 0, where BSP-17.3 reads node 0. `qs-bsp` writes the result as BSP-20.15 does.

A BSP29 clipnode child is read unsigned and is a clipnode when it is below the clipnode count, otherwise it less 65536, a negative contents value: `out->children[0] = (unsigned short)LittleShort(ins->children[0]);` then `if (out->children[0] >= count)` `out->children[0] -= 65536;` (`//johnfitz -- support clipnodes > 32k`). No BSP29 child fails, and a map of more than 32768 clipnodes can name those above 32767. GLQuake reads the child signed and uses one past the clipnodes unchecked, which this spec fails (BSP-1.8). BSP2 clipnode children are read as BSP-17.3 says (QS: `//Spike: FIXME: bounds check`).

These differences change no result `qs-bsp` gives: QS loads the entities before the textures, and no entity text fails to load; it appends a NUL to the entity text, which BSP-2.2 already ends at the lump; `Mod_DecompressVis` stops a run at the end of the row (`Mod_DecompressVis: output overrun on model`) and grows its row buffer, where id's writes past the row into a buffer of `MAX_MAP_LEAFS/8` bytes, and BSP-6.3 keeps the row's bytes only, for every loader; it warns about more than 32767 faces, nodes, clipnodes or marksurfaces, more than 8192 `visleafs`, and a face of fewer than 3 edges; its messages for some lumps of the wrong size, and for a bad marksurface, name other functions (`Mod_ProcessLeafs: funny lump size in %s`, `Mod_LoadClipnodes: funny lump size in %s`, `Mod_LoadMarksurfaces: bad surface number`), where `qs-bsp` gives id's message for every loader; and it reads the files beside the map that BSP-18 (`.lit`) and BSP-19 (`.ent`) describe, and a `.vis` file when its `external_vis` cvar is set, which `Bsp::read` does not open.

QS tells a leaf from a node as id does (BSP-12.7): its `Mod_SetParent` has `if (node->contents < 0)` `return;`, its `Mod_MakeHull0` `if (child->contents < 0)`, and its `mnode_t` and `mleaf_t` (`Quake/gl_model.h`) share the layout BSP-12.7 describes, with `out->efrags = NULL;` in each `Mod_ProcessLeafs_` function. So a leaf whose `contents` is 0 or more crashes QS when node 0's tree reaches it, and gives an undefined hull 0 child when only another model's nodes name it; that includes leaf 0 when BSP-20.15 or BSP-20.16 puts it in place of a leaf that does not exist. `qs-bsp` fails such a BSP with the default loader as with id's, after reading the children by BSP-20.15 and BSP-20.16.
id's table has the 79 entries numbered 0 to 78 (LIMIT-5.1). The builtin with number `n` is the C function in the table of BUILTIN-5 for `n`, whatever the progs calls the function.

Numbers 5, 33, 39, 42, 50, 60 to 66 and 71 have no builtin: the table holds `PF_Fixme` there, and calling one fails with the runtime error `unimplemented bulitin` (id's spelling). Number 0 cannot be called (LIMIT-5.2); 79 and above fail as LIMIT-5.1 says.

A builtin reads its parameters from the parameter slots whatever the argument count of the call (VM-14.1): a parameter the call did not supply is whatever the slot held (VM-14.6). Only the builtins that join their string parameters (BUILTIN-7.3) read the argument count.

A builtin that returns a value writes it to `RETURN` (one slot, or three for a vector). A builtin that returns nothing leaves the return slots unchanged unless a statement below says otherwise; unlike a QuakeC function (VM-16.2), it does not clear them.

A builtin runs to completion within the call statement: no frame is pushed (VM-14.4). The builtins that call back into QuakeC (`walkmove` and `movetogoal`, through touch functions) do so as nested runs (VM-18).
A builtin that fails may already have written globals, fields or engine state; where it has, the statement below says what is written before the check.
A float argument used as an integer (a channel, a style, a destination, a byte to write) is converted by C's float-to-int conversion, which truncates toward zero: 1.9 is 1 and -1.9 is -1.

A float outside the range of a 32-bit int, or a NaN, makes that conversion undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer as the x86 one (`cvttss2si`, `cvttsd2si`): the result is -2147483648 (0x80000000). Every conversion in this file follows this rule.

**Withdrawn** 2026-10-16: it said the builtin fails before it writes anything, but the check is made where id's code reads the value (BUILTIN-2.9), after whatever the builtin writes first; replaced by BUILTIN-2.7.

An entity argument read with `G_EDICTNUM` (or passed to `NUM_FOR_EDICT`) fails with the fatal error `NUM_FOR_EDICT: bad pointer` (BUILTIN-3.3) when its edict number is not less than `num_edicts` (EDICT-1.7). The statements below say which builtins do this.

A string argument is the text at the string value (PROGS-17.2, EDICT-13.1), read up to its NUL. A value that is neither inside the string table nor an engine-made string reads other memory, which is undefined in C; this spec fixes the answer: the builtin fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7).

A builtin that keeps a string argument (`setmodel`, the precache builtins, `lightstyle`) keeps the reference, not a copy of the text, so it sees later changes to that text, such as a new `ftos` result (BUILTIN-7.4).

An entity value a builtin reads with `G_EDICT`, `G_EDICTNUM` or `PROG_TO_EDICT`, from a parameter, a global (`self`, `msg_entity`) or a field (`goalentity`, `enemy`), is not checked by id's code: `PROG_TO_EDICT` adds it to the start of the edict array. A value that names no edict (EDICT-1.9) makes the builtin read or write memory that is not an edict, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: the builtin fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7) where it reads the value (BUILTIN-2.9). A value that names an edict passes, even one at or above `num_edicts` or a free one.

A string value is valid when it is from 0 to `numstrings - 1`, an offset into the string table (including one into the middle of a string, PROGS-11.3), or exactly the value of an engine-made string (EDICT-13.1, BUILTIN-7.4). Every other value is BUILTIN-2.5's invalid string: a negative one, `numstrings` or more outside the engine-made strings, and one that points past the start of an engine-made string's text, whose number depends on where the engine put that text (EDICT-13.3). A valid value's text is read up to its NUL (PROGS-11.1).

The entity check of BUILTIN-2.7, the string check of BUILTIN-2.5 and BUILTIN-2.8, and the field check of BUILTIN-8.3 are made where id's code reads the value, at each `G_EDICT`, `G_EDICTNUM`, `PROG_TO_EDICT`, `G_STRING` and `E_STRING` and at `makestatic`'s read of `model` (BUILTIN-12.8), in the order id's code reads them. So a builtin that fails one has already done what id's code does before that read: `changelevel` has recorded that it was issued (BUILTIN-11.6) and `makestatic` has appended `svc_spawnstatic`. A value the builtin does not read is not checked: `changelevel` reads no string once one was issued, and `find` reads the field of only the edicts it examines (BUILTIN-8.8). Of two bad values, the one read first decides the error: `setmodel(e, m)` reads `e` before `m`. `G_EDICTNUM` checks the entity before `NUM_FOR_EDICT` (BUILTIN-2.4) does, so a value that names no edict is the runtime error and a value that names an edict at or above `num_edicts` is the fatal error.

`WriteString(to, s)` and `WriteEntity(to, e)` read the destination (`WriteDest`, BUILTIN-13.1) and the value as two arguments of one C call (`MSG_WriteString (WriteDest(), G_STRING(OFS_PARM1))`, `MSG_WriteShort (WriteDest(), G_EDICTNUM(OFS_PARM1))`), and C leaves the order in which a call's arguments are evaluated unspecified, so which of two failures comes first depends on the compiler. This spec fixes the answer: the destination is read first, so with a bad destination and a bad value the error is the destination's.
A **runtime error** is `PR_RunError` with the message given: VM-19.1, VM-19.2 and VM-19.6 say what they do.

A **host error** is a call to `Host_Error ("Program error")` without `PR_RunError`: the aborted runs never continue (VM-19.2) and the server shuts down, but no statement or call stack is printed and the call depth is not reset to 0, unlike VM-19.1. The shutdown runs `ClientDisconnect` for every spawned client (`Host_ShutdownServer`, `SV_DropClient`), and those runs start at the depth the error left. Only `error` and `objerror` raise it.

A **fatal error** is `Sys_Error`: the engine prints the message and exits. In QuakeC Studio it ends the run with a typed error carrying the message, as a runtime error does, and nothing after it runs.
A **console message** is text printed to the server console (`Con_Printf`) after which the builtin returns normally; the run continues.
Class **pure**: the builtin reads and writes only the VM state (globals, edicts, the builtins' string buffers) and, for `random`, a random source. A mock that implements its statements is exact.

Class **state**: the builtin also reads or writes engine state that a fixture can hold as plain data: the precache lists and the bounds of each precached model, the lightstyles, the cvars, the client slots with their spawn parms, the server's `maxclients`, its state (loading or active), its clock and the `changelevel` flag. A mock with that fixture is exact for everything QuakeC can observe.

Class **output**: the builtin's effect outside the VM is output only: bytes appended to a network message buffer, console text, or text for a command buffer. A mock records the output, and is exact for everything QuakeC can observe, including the failures that depend on buffer sizes when it keeps the sizes of BUILTIN-13.

Class **world**: the builtin needs the map's collision hulls, the area tree of linked edicts or the PVS. It cannot be mocked faithfully without the server simulation (`qs-sim`, P3-24); `qc-builtins` marks it engine-only, and [`differential.md`](differential.md) says what the deterministic mock returns instead.

The vanilla builtins are numbers 1 to 78 in the table below. The prototype is the one in id's 1.01 `defs.qc`; the C function is the `pr_builtin` entry for that number; the class is BUILTIN-4's; the section is where its behaviour is specified. Numbers marked "none" are `PF_Fixme` (BUILTIN-1.2).

Three numbers have two names in `defs.qc` and one C function each: `precache_model2` (75) is `PF_precache_model`, `precache_sound2` (76) is `PF_precache_sound` and `precache_file2` (77) is `PF_precache_file`. id's comment on 76: "precache_sound2 is different only for qcc".

`makevectors(ang)` writes the globals `v_forward`, `v_right` and `v_up` and nothing else. With `angle = (f32)(a * (M_PI*2/360))` computed in double for each component `a`, and `sy`, `cy`, `sp`, `cp`, `sr`, `cr` the f32 sine and cosine (computed in double) of the yaw (`ang_y`), pitch (`ang_x`) and roll (`ang_z`) angles, in f32 arithmetic: `v_forward = (cp*cy, cp*sy, -sp)`, `v_right = (-1*sr*sp*cy + -1*cr*-sy, -1*sr*sp*sy + -1*cr*cy, -1*sr*cp)`, `v_up = (cr*sp*cy + -sr*-sy, cr*sp*sy + -sr*cy, cr*cp)`. Zero angles give `v_forward = '1 0 -0'`: the sign of a zero is kept.
`vlen(v)` returns `(f32)sqrt(x*x + y*y + z*z)`, the sum in f32 and the square root in double.

`normalize(v)` computes the length as `vlen` does. If it is 0 the result is `'0 0 0'`; otherwise it computes `inv = (f32)(1/len)` and returns `(x*inv, y*inv, z*inv)` in f32. A vector whose squared components all underflow to 0 in f32 has length 0, so a very short vector also gives `'0 0 0'`.

`vectoyaw(v)` returns 0 when `v_x` and `v_y` are both 0 (either sign). Otherwise it computes `atan2(v_y, v_x) * 180 / M_PI` in double, truncates it toward zero to an integer, and adds 360 if the result is negative: the result is a whole number from 0 to 359, and -179.4 degrees gives 181, not 180.

`vectoangles(v)` returns `'pitch yaw 0'`. When `v_x` and `v_y` are both 0 the yaw is 0 and the pitch is 90 if `v_z > 0` and 270 otherwise, so `'0 0 0'` gives `'270 0 0'`. Otherwise the yaw is `vectoyaw`'s, and the pitch is `atan2(v_z, (f32)sqrt(v_x*v_x + v_y*v_y))` in degrees, truncated toward zero, plus 360 if negative.

`random()` returns `(rand() & 0x7fff) / (f32)0x7fff`: one of the 32768 values `k / 32767` for `k` from 0 to 32767, so both 0 and 1 can be returned (id's comment "0<= num < 1" is wrong). Each call takes one number from the C library's `rand`, which the engine also uses elsewhere (`movetogoal`, BUILTIN-15.6); the sequence is the C library's and is not part of this spec. A mock takes the 15-bit values from an injected source.

`rint(f)` returns `(int)(f + 0.5)` when `f > 0` and `(int)(f - 0.5)` otherwise, the sum in double and the conversion truncating (BUILTIN-2.1, BUILTIN-2.2): halves round away from zero (2.5 gives 3, -2.5 gives -3), and 0 and -0 give +0.
`floor(f)` and `ceil(f)` return C's `floor` and `ceil` of `f` (in double, exact) rounded to f32, so the sign of a zero is kept: `ceil(-0.5)` is -0. `fabs(f)` returns `f` with the sign bit cleared.

`sin`, `cos`, `atan2` and `sqrt` are the C library's, in double. `sqrt` is exact; the others can differ in the last bit of the double between C libraries, which almost never survives the rounding to f32. This spec takes the results of the reference build (the oracle's C library on x86-64, P1-11); a mock uses Rust's `f64` functions, and a vector where they disagree after rounding is listed in `differential.md` as an expected difference.

`ftos(f)` returns `f` as decimal text: when `f == (int)f` (BUILTIN-2.2 for the conversion) it is `printf("%d", (int)f)`, so 1 gives `1` and -0 gives `0`; otherwise `printf("%5.1f", f)`: one decimal, rounded as C's `printf` rounds the exact binary value, right aligned in at least 5 characters, so 0.5 gives ` 0.5` and 1.25 gives ` 1.2`.
`vtos(v)` returns `printf("'%5.1f %5.1f %5.1f'", v_x, v_y, v_z)`: `'0 0 0'` gives `' 0.0 0.0 0.0'`, with the single quotes.

`error`, `objerror`, `bprint` and `dprint` use the text of every string parameter from PARM0 to the last one the call supplied, joined with nothing between; `sprint` and `centerprint` do the same from PARM1. The argument count decides how many (VM-14.1): a call with more arguments than the prototype prints them all, and one with none gives empty text.

`ftos` and `vtos` write their text into one engine buffer and return a string value for it (an engine-made string, EDICT-13.1); every call returns the same value, so the text of an earlier result changes when either builtin is called again. A mock keeps one such buffer.

id's buffers have fixed sizes: 128 bytes for `ftos` and `vtos`, 256 for the joined text of BUILTIN-7.3. Text longer than the buffer overflows it, which is undefined in C; `vtos` reaches it only with components of magnitude about 1e38 (130 characters for three `-3.4e38`). This spec fixes the answer: the text is never truncated, and the result is the full text.
`ftos` of a NaN or an infinity is printed by the C library, and C libraries differ (MSVC's text is not C99's). This spec fixes the answer as ` nan` for every NaN, ` inf` and ` -inf`.

`vtos` prints each component the way `ftos` prints a value that is not whole (BUILTIN-7.2), and a NaN or infinite component, which `%5.1f` leaves to the C library as BUILTIN-7.6 says, as ` nan` for every NaN, ` inf` and ` -inf`: `vtos` of a vector whose components are a NaN, an infinity and minus infinity is `' nan inf -inf'`.
`spawn()` allocates an edict by EDICT-6 and returns it, failing as EDICT-6.2 says when none is left (a fatal error, BUILTIN-3.3).
`remove(e)` frees `e` by EDICT-7. It refuses nothing: the world, a client edict and an edict that is already free are freed too (EDICT-4.6, EDICT-7.4).

`find(start, fld, match)` looks at edicts from `start`'s number plus 1 up to `num_edicts - 1`, skips free ones, and returns the first whose string field `fld` has the same text as `match` (byte comparison, `strcmp`); it returns the world when none does. The world itself is never examined, and a field value of 0 is the empty string, so `match` `""` finds edicts whose field is unset. `start` is read with `G_EDICTNUM` (BUILTIN-2.4); `fld` is a field index used without a check, which is undefined in C outside `0` to `entityfields - 1` and fails with a runtime error in this spec (VM-11.4).

`nextent(e)` returns the first edict after `e`, by number, that is not free, and the world when it reaches `num_edicts`. `nextent(world)` starts at edict 1, so client edicts are included. `e` is read with `G_EDICTNUM`.

`findradius(org, rad)` looks at edicts 1 to `num_edicts - 1` in order, skipping those that are free or whose `solid` is `SOLID_NOT` (0). For each other edict it computes, per axis, `d = org - (origin + (mins + maxs) * 0.5)` with `mins + maxs` in f32 and the rest in double, rounded to f32, and the length of `d` as `vlen` does; the edict is included unless that length is greater than `rad`, so one exactly at `rad` is included and none is when `rad` is a NaN.

`findradius` links the included edicts through their `chain` field in reverse order of number: it returns the last one included, whose `chain` is the one included before it, and so on, and the first one included has `chain` world. It returns the world when none is included. The `chain` of an edict not included is not changed.

`setspawnparms(e)` copies the 16 saved spawn parms of `e`'s client slot to the globals `parm1` to `parm16` (EDICT-11.9). `e` goes through `NUM_FOR_EDICT` (BUILTIN-2.4); an edict number outside 1 to `maxclients` fails with the runtime error `Entity is not a client`. It does not check that a player is connected to that slot.

`find` reads `start` (BUILTIN-2.4), then `match`, then, for each edict it examines (BUILTIN-8.3), the field `fld` with `E_STRING` before comparing: it checks that `fld` is a field slot (`invalid field`, BUILTIN-8.3) and that the field's value is a valid string (BUILTIN-2.8; `invalid string`). So it fails at the first examined edict whose field value is not a valid string, even when a later edict would match; it returns a match found before such an edict; and when it examines no edict (`start` is the last edict in use, or every edict after it is free) it checks neither `fld` nor any field value. id's checks for a null `match` (`PF_Find: bad search string`) and a null field text never fire: a string value never gives a null pointer.

`setorigin(e, o)` sets `e`'s `origin` to `o` and links `e` into the area tree without touching triggers, which writes `absmin` and `absmax` as EDICT-12.2 says (not for the world or a free edict). Linking without triggers runs no QuakeC.

`setsize(e, min, max)` fails with the runtime error `backwards mins/maxs` when `min` is greater than `max` on any axis, checked x, y, z, before writing anything; a NaN component passes the check. Otherwise it sets `mins` to `min`, `maxs` to `max` and `size` to `max - min` (f32), and links `e` as `setorigin` does. The box is never rotated: id's `rotate` argument is forced to false ("FIXME: implement rotation properly again").

`setmodel(e, m)` looks for `m`'s text in the model precache list from entry 0 and fails with the runtime error `no precache: <m>` followed by a newline when it is not there. Entry 0 is the empty string, so `setmodel(e, "")` finds entry 0.

It then sets `e`'s `model` to the string value `m` itself (not the list's copy, BUILTIN-2.6) and `modelindex` to the entry number, and sets the size as `setsize` does from the model's bounds: for entry 0, or an entry with no loaded model, `'0 0 0'` for both; for an alias model (`.mdl`) `'-16 -16 -16'` and `'16 16 16'`; for a sprite (`.spr`) `-w/2` to `w/2` on x and y and `-h/2` to `h/2` on z, from its largest frame width `w` and height `h` in integer arithmetic (an odd width loses its half); for the world (entry 1) and its submodels (`*1`, `*2`, ...) the bounds stored in the BSP file, widened by 1 on each side by `Mod_LoadSubmodels`. A model's bounds never trip `backwards mins/maxs`.

`precache_sound(s)` and `precache_model(s)` fail with the runtime error `PF_Precache_*: Precache can only be done in spawn functions` unless the server is loading: from the start of `SV_SpawnServer` until the map's entities have spawned (EDICT-8). The check comes first.

They then set `RETURN` to `s` (the same string value), and fail with the runtime error `Bad string` when the first byte of `s` is a space or below, read as a signed `char` as on x86: an empty string, one starting with a control character or a space, and one starting with a byte from 0x80 to 0xFF all fail.

They look through the list from entry 0: a name already there does nothing; otherwise `s` (the reference, BUILTIN-2.6) goes in the first unused entry. A full list fails as LIMIT-6.2 says. When the map starts, the sound list holds only entry 0 (the empty string) and the model list holds entry 0, the world model `maps/<map>.bsp` in entry 1 and its submodels `*1`, `*2`, ... after it, so precaching any of those names does nothing.
`precache_model` loads a newly added model at once; a file that cannot be found is the fatal error `Mod_NumForName: <s> not found`. `precache_sound` does not load anything.
`precache_file(s)` sets `RETURN` to `s` and does nothing else, at any time; id's comment: "precache_file is only used to copy files with qcc, it does nothing".
`precache_model2`, `precache_sound2` and `precache_file2` behave exactly as `precache_model`, `precache_sound` and `precache_file` (BUILTIN-5.2).
`bprint(s)` appends `svc_print` (8) and the joined text (BUILTIN-7.3) with its NUL to the reliable message of every client slot that is active and spawned.

`sprint(client, s)` and `centerprint(client, s)` read `client` with `G_EDICTNUM` (BUILTIN-2.4). When its number is outside 1 to `maxclients` they print the console message `tried to sprint to a non-client` (both builtins) and return. Otherwise they append `svc_print` (8) or `svc_centerprint` (26), then the joined text from PARM1 with its NUL, to that slot's reliable message, whether or not a player is connected to it.
`dprint(s)` prints the joined text to the console only when the `developer` setting is non-zero, and does nothing otherwise.

`stuffcmd(client, s)` reads `client` with `G_EDICTNUM`; a number outside 1 to `maxclients` fails with the runtime error `Parm 0 not a client`. Otherwise it appends `svc_stufftext` (9) and `s` with its NUL to that slot's reliable message, connected or not; the client runs the text as console commands. No newline is added.

`localcmd(s)` appends `s`, without its NUL and without adding a newline, to the server's own command buffer (8192 bytes), which the host runs later, not during the call. If the buffer's contents plus `s` would reach 8192 bytes it prints the console message `Cbuf_AddText: overflow` and drops `s`.

`changelevel(s)` does nothing if a `changelevel` was already issued since the map started. Otherwise it records that one was, and appends `changelevel <s>` and a newline to the command buffer as `localcmd` does; the level changes when the host next runs its command buffer, not during the call.

`cvar(s)` returns the value of the setting named `s`, or 0 when there is no such setting. The value is the setting's text converted by `Q_atof`: an optional `-`, then a hexadecimal number after `0x` or `0X`, the code of the character after a `'`, or decimal digits with at most one `.`, stopping at the first other character, with no exponent and no leading spaces (`"1e3"` is 1, `" 5"` is 0).

`cvar_set(var, val)` sets the setting named `var` to the text `val` and its value to `Q_atof(val)`. An unknown name prints the console message `Cvar_Set: variable <var> not found` and changes nothing. When the setting is a server setting, the text changed and the server is active, it also broadcasts `"<var>" changed to "<val>"` and a newline as `bprint` does.

`sound(e, chan, samp, vol, atten)` converts `chan` to an integer (BUILTIN-2.1) and `vol * 255` (f32) to an integer volume, and fails with the fatal errors `SV_StartSound: volume = <volume>` when the volume is outside 0 to 255, `SV_StartSound: attenuation = <atten>` when `atten` is outside 0 to 4, and `SV_StartSound: channel = <chan>` when the channel is outside 0 to 7, checked in that order. A NaN `atten` passes its check.

Then, when the unreliable datagram (BUILTIN-13.3) holds more than `MAX_DATAGRAM - 16` (1008) bytes, the sound is dropped silently. When `samp` is not in the sound precache list, looked up from entry 1, it prints the console message `SV_StartSound: <samp> not precacheed` (id's spelling) and returns. `e` goes through `NUM_FOR_EDICT` (BUILTIN-2.4) after these checks.

Otherwise it appends to the unreliable datagram: `svc_sound` (6); a byte of flags, 1 when the volume is not 255 and 2 when `atten` is not 1.0; the volume as a byte if flag 1; `atten * 64` as a byte if flag 2 (its low 8 bits, BUILTIN-13.2, so an `atten` of 4 is sent as 0); a short `(edict number << 3) | channel`; the sound's precache entry as a byte; and three coordinates (BUILTIN-13.2), the centre of `e`, `origin + 0.5 * (mins + maxs)` per axis.

`ambientsound(pos, samp, vol, atten)` looks for `samp` in the sound precache list from entry 0; when it is not there it prints the console message `no precache: <samp>` and returns. Otherwise it appends to the signon buffer: `svc_spawnstaticsound` (29), three coordinates of `pos`, the entry number as a byte, `vol * 255` as a byte and `atten * 64` as a byte. Every map's client receives the signon buffer when it connects.

`particle(o, d, color, count)` does nothing when the unreliable datagram holds more than 1008 bytes. Otherwise it appends `svc_particle` (18), three coordinates of `o`, for each axis of `d` the integer `(int)(d * 16)` clamped to -128 to 127 as a char, then `count` as a byte and `color` as a byte, both converted by BUILTIN-2.1.

`lightstyle(style, value)` converts `style` to an integer and stores `value` (the reference, BUILTIN-2.6) as that lightstyle. id does not check the style number against `LIMIT_MAX_LIGHTSTYLES` (64), so a number outside 0 to 63 writes outside the array, which is undefined in C; this spec fixes the answer: it fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7) before storing anything.

When the server is active, `lightstyle` also appends `svc_lightstyle` (12), the style as a char and `value` with its NUL to the reliable message of every client slot that is active or spawned. While the map loads it only stores the style, which clients get when they connect.

`makestatic(e)` appends to the signon buffer: `svc_spawnstatic` (20); the model's precache entry as a byte, found by the text of `e`'s `model` (0 for an empty model, and the fatal error `SV_ModelIndex: model <model> not precached` when the text is not in the list); `frame`, `colormap` and `skin` as bytes; then for x, y and z in turn the coordinate of `origin` and the angle of `angles` (BUILTIN-13.2). Then it frees `e` (EDICT-7.5).

The `Write*` builtins convert `to` to an integer and append to: 0 (`MSG_BROADCAST`) the unreliable datagram; 1 (`MSG_ONE`) the reliable message of the client slot of the edict in the global `msg_entity`, which goes through `NUM_FOR_EDICT` (BUILTIN-2.4) and fails with the runtime error `WriteDest: not a client` when its number is outside 1 to `maxclients`; 2 (`MSG_ALL`) the reliable datagram; 3 (`MSG_INIT`) the signon buffer. Any other value fails with the runtime error `WriteDest: bad destination`.

The value is written little-endian: `WriteByte` and `WriteChar` write the low 8 bits of the integer conversion of `f` (BUILTIN-2.1), `WriteShort` the low 16 bits, `WriteLong` all 32; `WriteCoord` writes the low 16 bits of `(int)(f * 8)`, the product in f32; `WriteAngle` writes `((int)f * 256 / 360) & 255` in integer arithmetic, so the angle is truncated to whole degrees first and the division truncates toward zero (-90 gives 192); `WriteString` writes the text and its NUL; `WriteEntity` writes the edict number of `s` (through `NUM_FOR_EDICT`, BUILTIN-2.4) as a short. No value is range checked: `PARANOID` is off.

The unreliable datagram and the reliable datagram are `LIMIT_MAX_DATAGRAM` (1024) bytes and the signon buffer is 8192; they are cleared for each map (the datagrams also after each frame's updates are sent). A write that does not fit is the fatal error `SZ_GetSpace: overflow without allowoverflow set`.

A client slot's reliable message is `LIMIT_MAX_MSGLEN` (8000) bytes and may overflow: a write that does not fit prints the console message `SZ_GetSpace: overflow`, empties the message, marks it overflowed and then writes; the server drops that client when it next sends updates. The run continues.

`traceline(v1, v2, nomonsters, forent)` traces a point from `v1` to `v2` through the world and the linked edicts whose `solid` is not `SOLID_NOT`. It ignores `forent`, every edict whose `owner` is `forent`, `forent`'s own `owner`, and, when `forent`'s `size_x` is not 0, every edict whose `size_x` is 0. `forent` is never "none": when it is the world, every edict whose `owner` is the world (0) is ignored, so only the map and edicts with an owner can be hit. `nomonsters` is converted to an integer: 1 (`MOVE_NOMONSTERS`) also ignores every edict whose `solid` is not `SOLID_BSP`; 2 (`MOVE_MISSILE`) traces a box of `'-15 -15 -15'` to `'15 15 15'` instead of a point against edicts whose `flags` have `FL_MONSTER` (32); any other value is a normal trace.

`traceline` writes all nine `trace_*` globals (EDICT-11.11): `trace_allsolid`, `trace_startsolid`, `trace_inopen` and `trace_inwater` as 0 or 1, `trace_fraction`, `trace_endpos`, `trace_plane_normal`, `trace_plane_dist`, and `trace_ent`, the edict hit or the world when nothing was hit. It returns nothing; the 1.01 prototype `void(...)` agrees.

`checkclient()` returns a client edict that `self` might see, or the world. When at least 0.1 seconds of server time have passed since it last chose, it chooses again: starting after the last choice, it cycles through client edicts 1 to `maxclients` and takes the first that is not free, has `health` above 0 and has no `FL_NOTARGET` (128) in `flags`, or the last choice again if no other qualifies, and stores the PVS at that client's `origin + view_ofs`. It returns the world when the chosen edict is free or its `health` is 0 or less, or when the leaf at `self`'s `origin + view_ofs` is not in the stored PVS; otherwise the chosen edict.

`pointcontents(v)` returns the contents of the world model's point hull at `v`: `CONTENTS_EMPTY` (-1), `CONTENTS_SOLID` (-2), `CONTENTS_WATER` (-3), `CONTENTS_SLIME` (-4), `CONTENTS_LAVA` (-5) or `CONTENTS_SKY` (-6). The current contents -9 to -14 are returned as `CONTENTS_WATER`. Entities are not considered.

`checkbottom(e)` returns 1 when `SV_CheckBottom` finds `e`'s bounding box supported and 0 otherwise: supported when the world is solid 1 unit below each bottom corner, or when traces down from the bottom centre and from each bottom corner all hit within 36 units (two steps) and no corner's floor is more than 18 units (`BUILTIN_STEPSIZE`) below the centre's. It writes nothing.

`aim(e, speed)` ignores `speed` and returns a direction for `e` to shoot along, reading `v_forward`, the `teamplay` and `sv_aim` (0.93) settings and the `takedamage` and `team` fields: `v_forward` itself when a trace from `e`'s origin plus 20 units up along `v_forward` for 2048 units hits an edict with `takedamage` `DAMAGE_AIM` (2) that is not a teammate. Otherwise it picks, among the edicts with `takedamage` `DAMAGE_AIM` other than `e` and its teammates, the one whose centre has the largest dot product with `v_forward` from that start point, at least `sv_aim`, among those a trace to the centre reaches; and returns `v_forward` scaled by the dot product of `v_forward` with the difference of the two edicts' `origin`s, with its z replaced by that difference's z, normalized. With no such edict it returns `v_forward`. It writes nothing.

`walkmove(yaw, dist)` acts on `self`. When `self`'s `flags`, converted to an integer, has none of `FL_ONGROUND` (512), `FL_FLY` (1) and `FL_SWIM` (2), it returns 0 and changes nothing. Otherwise it tries to move `self` by `(cos(y) * dist, sin(y) * dist, 0)` with `y = (f32)(yaw * M_PI * 2 / 360)`, stepping up and down stairs (18 units) and refusing to walk off an edge, flying and swimming monsters adjusting height toward their `enemy`, and returns 1 if it moved and 0 if not.

A successful `walkmove` writes `origin`, may write `groundentity` and clear `FL_PARTIALGROUND` (EDICT-12.13, EDICT-12.18), and relinks `self` touching triggers, which can run their `touch` functions as nested runs (BUILTIN-1.5). After the move it restores the global `self` and the current function to what they were before; it does not restore `other` or any other global a touch function changed.

`droptofloor()` acts on `self` and ignores its parameters (the 1.01 prototype declares two; the rerelease's declares none). It traces `self`'s box from `origin` to 256 units below, as a normal move ignoring `self`. When the trace is all in solid or hits nothing it returns 0 and changes nothing. Otherwise it sets `origin` to the end of the trace, links `self` without touching triggers, sets `FL_ONGROUND` in `flags`, sets `groundentity` to the edict hit (the world for the map) and returns 1.

`ChangeYaw()` turns `self`'s yaw toward `ideal_yaw` by at most `yaw_speed`, in f32: `current = anglemod(angles_y)`; if `current == ideal_yaw` it changes nothing. Otherwise `move = ideal_yaw - current`, minus 360 when `ideal_yaw > current` and `move >= 180`, plus 360 when `ideal_yaw <= current` and `move <= -180`; then clamped to `yaw_speed` when positive and to `-yaw_speed` when not; and `angles_y` becomes `anglemod(current + move)`.

`anglemod(a)` is `(360.0/65536) * ((int)(a * (65536/360.0)) & 65535)` in double, rounded to f32: the angle is wrapped to 0 up to 360 and truncated toward zero to a multiple of 360/65536 degrees, so `ChangeYaw` can leave `angles_y` a little short of `ideal_yaw` (20 becomes 19.995117) and can change it even when it is already equal to `ideal_yaw` unless `ideal_yaw` is such a multiple.

`movetogoal(step)` acts on `self` and its `goalentity`. When `self` is not on the ground, flying or swimming (as `walkmove` checks) it writes 0 to `RETURN` and changes nothing else. When `self`'s `enemy` is not the world and `self`'s `absmin` and `absmax` widened by `step` overlap the goal's, it does nothing. Otherwise it tries a step of `step` toward `ideal_yaw`, unless `rand() & 3` is 1; when it did not try or the step failed, it chooses a new direction toward the goal, trying the eight 45-degree headings in an order that also uses `rand()`, and sets `ideal_yaw` to the heading taken. Each try sets `ideal_yaw`, turns `self` as `ChangeYaw` does, steps as `walkmove` does without touching triggers, keeps the step only if `angles_y - ideal_yaw` after the turn is not strictly between 45 and 315, and then relinks `self` touching triggers. It writes `angles`, `ideal_yaw`, `origin`, `groundentity` and `flags` (EDICT-12.20).

`error(s)` prints `======SERVER ERROR in <function>:`, a newline, the joined text (BUILTIN-7.3) and a newline, where `<function>` is the name of the QuakeC function that called it; then it prints `self` as `eprint` does and raises a host error (BUILTIN-3.2).

`objerror(s)` prints `======OBJECT ERROR in <function>:` and the text in the same way, prints `self`, frees `self` (EDICT-7.5), then raises a host error. id's comment says "the level can continue", but the code stops the server as `error` does.

`break()` prints the console message `break statement` and then writes to address -4 ("dump to debugger"), which crashes the engine. This spec fixes the answer: after the message it is the fatal error `break statement` (BUILTIN-3.3).
`traceon()` and `traceoff()` set and clear the VM's statement trace flag (VM-2.3, VM-18.3). They change no global or field.

`eprint(e)` prints `e`'s fields to the console as `ED_Print` formats them, and `coredump()` prints `num_edicts` and then every edict from 0 to `num_edicts - 1` the same way. `e` goes through `NUM_FOR_EDICT` (BUILTIN-2.4). The text is not part of this spec; they change nothing QuakeC can observe.

For every number from 1 to 78 that the rerelease's `defs.qc` declares, it uses the name and number of BUILTIN-5, and the same prototype except as BUILTIN-17.2 and BUILTIN-17.3 say. It leaves 5, 33, 39, 42, 50, 60 to 66 and 71 undeclared, as the 1.01 `defs.qc` does.

The rerelease declares `droptofloor` as `float()`, where 1.01 declares `float(float yaw, float dist)`; the builtin ignores its parameters either way (BUILTIN-15.3). It declares `dprint` (25) as `void(string s, ...)`, which BUILTIN-7.3 already handles.

The rerelease declares no builtin with number 23, 24 or 73: `bprint`, `sprint` and `centerprint` are `#0:ex_bprint`, `#0:ex_sprint` and `#0:ex_centerprint`, variadic extension builtins the rerelease's engine finds by name. Its other `#0:ex_*` builtins and `checkextension` (`#99`) are not vanilla and are not in this spec; the engine target database (P2-04) covers them.

Every rerelease codebase compiles to a version 6 `progs.dat` (`progs.md` PROGS-2.1) whose statements all use opcodes 0 to 65, the opcodes id's VM has (`progs.md` PROGS-8.1). None uses an FTE extended opcode or the version 7 format. So the rerelease needs no extension to the progs format this project already reads; the dialect is a front-end concern, not a format one.

FTEQCC compiles the rerelease with `-Tid`, its target that refuses any opcode id's VM lacks. The mission-pack codebase Dawn of the Machine (`rerelease-mg3`) also needs `-Fautoproto`, because it uses functions and constants before it declares them, which FTEQCC resolves only when it collects prototypes in a first pass. Both facts are recorded by the oracle (`xtask/src/oracles/rerelease.rs`).

`for (init; cond; step) body` is a statement. `init` and `step` are expression statements (either may be empty), `cond` is an expression (an empty `cond` is always true), and `body` is one statement or a block.

`init` may be a local declaration with an initialiser: `for (float i = 0; ...)` declares `i` for the loop. The rerelease uses this form (`rerelease-mg1/misc_corpses.qc`, `rerelease-mg3/mg3_upgrades.qc`).
The loop runs `init` once, then while `cond` is true runs `body` then `step`. `continue` (FTE-4) jumps to `step`; `break` (FTE-4) leaves the loop.
Progs encoding: a `for` lowers to the statements of `while` (QC-22, QC-14.3): `init`; a test with `IFNOT` to after the loop; `body`; `step`; a `GOTO` back to the test. No new opcode is used.

`switch (expr) { ... }` selects among `case value:` labels and an optional `default:` label by comparing `expr` to each `case` value. A `case` value is a constant expression (the rerelease uses named float constants, for example `rerelease/itemnames.qc`).
Control enters at the first matching `case`, or at `default` if none matches and a `default` is present, or leaves the `switch` if none matches and there is no `default`.

Execution falls through from one label's statements into the next unless a `break` (FTE-4) leaves the `switch`. A `case` whose body is a block `{ ... }` is accepted (`rerelease/itemnames.qc` uses `case IT_KEY1: { ... }`).

Progs encoding: a `switch` lowers to a chain of equality tests and `GOTO`s over vanilla opcodes (`EQ_F` or the comparison for the switched type, `IFNOT`, `GOTO`), with no new opcode; a `break` becomes a `GOTO` to after the `switch`.

`break;` leaves the innermost enclosing `while`, `do`, `for` (FTE-2) or `switch` (FTE-3). `continue;` jumps to the next iteration of the innermost enclosing loop (its `step` in a `for`, or its condition test). The rerelease uses both (`rerelease/monsters/chthon.qc`, `rerelease-mg1/misc_fx.qc`).
A `break` or `continue` with no enclosing loop or switch is an error.
Progs encoding: each becomes a `GOTO` to the loop or switch's exit or continue point; no new opcode is used.

`lvalue++` and `lvalue--` are postfix expressions that read the lvalue, then store it plus or minus one. The rerelease uses `i++` in `for` loop steps (`rerelease-mg1/misc_corpses.qc`, `rerelease-mg3/mg3_upgrades.qc`).
As a statement the result is unused, so postfix and prefix have the same effect; the rerelease uses only the postfix form in a `for` step.
Progs encoding: `x++` lowers to `ADD_F x, 1` into a temporary and `STORE_F` back to `x` (or the field store for a field), over vanilla opcodes; no new opcode is used.

`lvalue += rhs`, `-=`, `*=` and `/=` read the lvalue, apply the operator with `rhs`, and store the result back. The rerelease uses all four on floats and vectors (`rerelease/ai.qc` `ang_x *= -1`, `rerelease-ctf/hook.qc` `start += offset`, `rerelease-mg1/math.qc` `num/= 2`).
The operand types follow the matching binary operator (QC-16): `+=` and `-=` on `float` or `vector`, `*=` with a `float` or vector-scale right side, `/=` by a `float`.
Progs encoding: `x += y` lowers to the binary op into a temporary and a store back to `x`, over vanilla opcodes (`ADD_F`/`ADD_V` and so on); no new opcode is used.
`a % b` is the floating-point remainder of `a` divided by `b`. The rerelease uses it on floats (`rerelease-mg1/horde.qc` `self.wave % 3`).
Division by zero follows FTEQCC's generated code; the exact result is fixed when P2-06 implements the lowering and is checked against the rerelease's runtime behaviour in the differential suite.

Progs encoding: `%` has no vanilla opcode, so FTEQCC emits a short sequence of vanilla float opcodes (a division, truncation and multiply-subtract). The exact statements are fixed by P2-06 and recorded in this section's vectors then.
