The end of the file where a name, a number or a required keyword is expected is an error; a list of entries (MD5-2.8, MD5-3.6) and the optional `commandline` just end there. QSS reads an empty token at the end and fails at the next keyword it requires, or reads 0 for a number; this spec fixes the answer as an error at the end of the file.
A mesh file's first four bytes are `MD5V`; `Mod_LoadModel` picks the MD5 loader by them, so a file that starts with anything else, even whitespace, is not read as MD5 and the reader rejects it.

The header is the tokens `MD5Version` and `10`, optionally `commandline` and one token, then `numJoints` and its count and `numMeshes` and its count. A missing or different keyword fails with the error `Expected "<keyword>"`.
`numJoints` must be at least 1 (`<name> has no bones`) and `numMeshes` at least 1 (`<name> has no meshes`).

`joints` and `{` follow, then exactly `numJoints` joints, then `}`. A joint is its name, its parent joint's index, `(`, a position of three floats, `)`, `(`, the x, y and z of its orientation quaternion, and `)`.

A joint's parent must be -1 (no parent) or the index of a joint, less than `numJoints`; otherwise reading fails with the error `bone index out of bounds`. QSS's test is `parent < -1 && parent >= numjoints`, which is never true, so QSS accepts any parent; this spec fixes the check it meant.
A quaternion's w is `-sqrt(1 - (x*x + y*y + z*z))` in `f32`, with the value under the root taken as 0 when it is negative, so w is never positive.

Exactly `numMeshes` meshes follow the joints. A mesh is `mesh`, `{`, `shader` and one token naming its skin, `numverts` and a count, the vertices, `numtris` and a count, the triangles, `numweights` and a count, the weights, and `}`. Tokens after the last mesh are ignored.

Vertices, triangles and weights are lists of entries, each starting with its keyword (`vert`, `tri`, `weight`) and its index; a list ends at the first token that is not the keyword. The count need not equal the number of entries: an index never given is all zero, and an index given twice keeps the last entry.

A vertex is `vert`, its index (less than `numverts`), `(`, texture coordinates `s` and `t` as floats, `)`, the index of its first weight and its number of weights. A vertex index of `numverts` or more fails with the error `vertex index out of bounds`.

A triangle is `tri`, its index (less than `numtris`, or the error `triangle index out of bounds`) and three vertex indices, each less than `numverts`, or the error `vertex index out of bounds`. QSS's test is `t > numverts`, which accepts `numverts` itself and reads one vertex past the array; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

A weight is `weight`, its index (less than `numweights`, or the error `weight index out of bounds`), its joint's index (less than `numJoints`, or the error `bone index out of bounds`), its bias as a float, `(`, a position of three floats, and `)`.

Each vertex's weights are the `count` weights from its first: first weight plus count must be at most `numweights` (the error `<name>: weight index out of bounds`). The check is made once the mesh's weights are read, for every vertex including those never given.

A mesh's skins are images found from its shader name: skin `n` frame `f` is `progs/<shader>_<nn>_<ff>`, with `n` and `f` written as two or more decimal digits (`progs/ogre_00_00`). QSS looks for skins from 0 and frames from 0 to 3, and stops at the first skin with no frame 0; the image file's extension is the image loader's.
The animation of `<path>.md5mesh` is `<path>.md5anim`, the same path with the extension replaced. A mesh with no animation file loads with no frames.

The header is the tokens `MD5Version` and `10`, optionally `commandline` and one token, `numFrames` and its count, `numJoints` and its count, `frameRate` and one token (the frame rate, which QSS skips without reading it as a number), then `numAnimatedComponents` and its count. `numFrames` must be at least 1 (`<name> has no poses`).

`hierarchy` and `{` follow, then exactly `numJoints` entries, then `}`. An entry is a joint name, its parent's index, its flags and the index of its first component. Flags other than the low six bits fail with the error `<name>: bone has unsupported flags`.

A joint's components are the ones its flags select, in the order x, y, z of the position then x, y, z of the quaternion, for flag bits 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32; they are read from its first component on. Its first component plus the number of flags set must be at most `numAnimatedComponents`, or reading fails with the error `<name>: bone has bad offset`. QSS only checks that the first component is at most `numAnimatedComponents + 6` and reads the six spare floats it allocates, or past them; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

`bounds` and `{` follow, then any number of pairs `(` x y z `)` `(` x y z `)`, then `}`; then `baseframe` and `{`, any number of pairs `(` x y z `)` `(` qx qy qz `)`, and `}`. Their counts are not checked, and QSS reads the values and does not use them.

Then come frames, each `frame`, its index (less than `numFrames`, or the error `<name>: invalid pose index`), `{`, exactly `numAnimatedComponents` floats and `}`. The list ends at the first token that is not `frame`, and tokens after it are ignored. A frame never given has every component 0, and a frame given twice keeps the last.

A joint's pose in a frame is its components as MD5-3.4 selects them, with each component its flags do not select taken as 0 (not from `baseframe`, as id Tech 4 does), and the quaternion's w computed as MD5-2.6 says.

The end of the file after `frameRate`'s value fails reading with the error `Expected "numAnimatedComponents"`. QSS then keeps the frame count with no poses, which is undefined when the model is drawn; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

An animation goes with a mesh only if its `numJoints` equals the mesh's (`<name> has incorrect bone count`) and each hierarchy entry has the name and parent of the mesh's joint at the same index (`<name>: bone was renamed`, `<name>: bone has wrong parent`).
Each frame of the animation is one frame of the model, shown for 0.1 seconds.

`numAnimatedComponents` must be at most the length of the file in bytes, up to its first NUL (MD5-1.1), or reading fails with the error `<name> has too many animated components`. A frame never given still has `numAnimatedComponents` components (MD5-3.6), so without a bound a file of a few bytes with no `frame` could ask for 2^64 of them. QSS sets no bound of its own: it allocates `raw = Z_Malloc(sizeof(*raw)*(rawcount+6));` from the count as read, which fails on a count its zone cannot hold and wraps for a count near 2^64. This spec's bound is stricter than QSS: QSS loads a file with no `frame` whose count is larger than the file but fits its zone, giving all-zero poses, and this spec refuses it. The bound refuses no file that gives a frame, since each of a frame's components is at least one byte and a separator.
An alias model starts with the 84-byte header above.

Its first four bytes are `IDPO` (0x49 0x44 0x50 0x4F). `Mod_LoadModel` sends a file that starts with them to the alias loader and any other to another loader (SPR-1.2, BSP-1.2); the alias reader rejects a file without them.
`version` must be 6; any other value fails with the error `<name> has wrong version number (<version> should be 6)` (fatal in id's engine).

Then, in this order, each failing with its error (fatal in id's engine): `skinheight` over 480 (`model <name> has a skin taller than 480`); `numverts` of 0 or less (`model <name> has no vertices`); `numverts` over 2000 (`model <name> has too many vertices`); `numtris` of 0 or less (`model <name> has no triangles`); `skinwidth` not a multiple of 4, tested as `skinwidth & 3` (`Mod_LoadAliasModel: skinwidth not multiple of 4`); `numskins` under 1 (`Mod_LoadAliasModel: Invalid # of skins: <numskins>`). The skins, texture coordinates and triangles are then read, and only after them `numframes` under 1 fails (`Mod_LoadAliasModel: Invalid # of frames: <numframes>`).

A negative `skinwidth` or `skinheight`, a skin size `skinwidth * skinheight` that does not fit in a signed 32-bit integer, or a file shorter than the header fails to load. id's code reads the header unchecked and uses these values as sizes, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error. (`-4 & 3` is 0, so the test of MDL-1.4 alone passes a negative width.)
`scale`, `scale_origin`, `boundingradius`, `eyeposition`, `synctype`, `flags` and `size` are not checked. The loader keeps `size` multiplied by `1.0 / 11.0`.
Every alias model's bounds are (-16, -16, -16) to (16, 16, 16), whatever its frames hold (`Mod_LoadAliasModel`: "FIXME: do this right").

GLQuake's loader (`WinQuake/gl_model.c`, `Mod_LoadAliasModel`, `Mod_LoadAllSkins`) checks `numframes` before the skins, rejects more than 1024 vertices and more than 32 skins (`Mod_LoadAliasModel: Invalid # of skins: <numskins>`), and does not check `skinwidth` or the intervals of MDL-2.3 and MDL-5.5. It keeps triangles and frame poses in fixed arrays of 2048 and 256 without checking either count. A model is loadable by GLQuake-derived engines only within those four limits; a reader reports a model that exceeds one.

`flags` holds the `EF_` bits that make the client draw an effect behind the entity or spin it: 1 rocket trail, 2 grenade trail, 4 gib trail, 8 rotate, 16 green split trail, 32 small blood trail, 64 orange split trail and rotate, 128 purple trail.

After the header come `numskins` skin entries, each starting with a 32-bit type. A type of 0 (`ALIAS_SKIN_SINGLE`) is followed by one skin; any other value, not only 1 (`ALIAS_SKIN_GROUP`), is followed by a skin group.
A skin is `skinwidth * skinheight` bytes of palette indices, row by row from the top left.

A skin group is a 32-bit count, then that many float intervals, then that many skins. Every interval must be greater than 0; one that is 0 or less fails with the error `Mod_LoadAliasSkinGroup: interval<=0` (fatal in id's engine). The test is `<= 0`, so a NaN interval loads.
A skin group's count must be at least 1. id's code allocates and reads with a count of 0 or less without checking it, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
A skin, interval or count that runs past the end of the file fails to load. id's code reads it unchecked, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
After the skins come `numverts` 12-byte `stvert_t` entries, one per vertex: `onseam`, then `s` and `t`, the vertex's position on the skin in pixels from the top left.

A skin holds the model's front on its left half and its back on its right half. A vertex with a non-zero `onseam` lies on the seam between them; when a triangle that does not face front (MDL-4.2) uses it, its `s` is moved right by `skinwidth / 2`. `modelgen.h` names the flag `ALIAS_ONSEAM` (0x20).
The software loader keeps `s` and `t` as 16.16 fixed point (`s << 16`), which is undefined in C for a value outside -32768 to 32767; this spec keeps them as the 32-bit values read.
After the texture coordinates come `numtris` 16-byte `dtriangle_t` entries: `facesfront`, then three vertex numbers, which index both the texture coordinates and each frame's vertices.
A `facesfront` of 0 marks a triangle on the back half of the skin; any other value faces front. `modelgen.h` defines `DT_FACES_FRONT` as 0x10.
A vertex number below 0 or not below `numverts` fails to load. id's code does not check them and the renderer indexes with them, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
After the triangles come `numframes` frame entries, each starting with a 32-bit type. A type of 0 (`ALIAS_SINGLE`) is followed by one frame; any other value is followed by a frame group.

A frame is a 24-byte `daliasframe_t` (its bounding box as two `trivertx_t`, whose `lightnormalindex` is unused, and a 16-byte name) followed by `numverts` `trivertx_t`, one per vertex. The name is the bytes before the first NUL, or all 16; id's code copies it with `strcpy`, which reads past a name with no NUL, undefined behaviour this spec settles that way.

A vertex's position in the model is `v[i] * scale[i] + scale_origin[i]` on each axis, in single precision, and its normal is entry `lightnormalindex` of the 162 precomputed normals in `r_avertexnormals`. An index of 162 or more reads past that table in id's renderer, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer: the model loads and the index is reported.

A frame group is a 12-byte `daliasgroup_t` (a 32-bit count and the group's bounding box), then that many float intervals, then that many frames as in MDL-5.2. The entry takes the group's bounding box, and its name is the name of the group's last frame, because each frame of the group is copied into the same name buffer.

Every interval of a frame group must be greater than 0; one that is 0 or less fails with the error `Mod_LoadAliasGroup: interval<=0` (fatal in id's engine). The test is `<= 0.0`, so a NaN interval loads. GLQuake does not check the intervals and keeps only the first.
A frame group's count must be at least 1, as MDL-2.4, and a frame, interval or count that runs past the end of the file fails to load, as MDL-2.5.
Bytes after the last frame entry are ignored.
A PAK file starts with a 12-byte header: the four bytes `PACK` (0x50 0x41 0x43 0x4B), then `dirofs` and `dirlen` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers.

If the first four bytes are not exactly `PACK` (the comparison is case-sensitive, so `pack` fails), loading fails with the error `<path> is not a packfile`. In id's engine this is a fatal `Sys_Error`.

A file of fewer than 12 bytes fails to load. id's code does not check the length of the read and decodes whatever was in the uninitialised header struct, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error, the same as PAK-1.2, because no valid archive is that short.
A PAK path that cannot be opened is not an error of the format: `COM_LoadPackFile` returns `NULL` and its caller decides what that means (FS-1.5, FS-2.2).
The directory is `dirlen` bytes at offset `dirofs`, holding 64-byte entries: a 56-byte name, then `filepos` and `filelen` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers.
The number of entries is `dirlen` divided by 64, rounded down. The remaining `dirlen % 64` bytes are not an entry; they are still read, and they count towards the CRC of PAK-4.1.
A `dirlen` from 0 to 63 gives an archive with no entries, which loads without error.
More than 2048 entries fails with the error `<path> has <n> files` (fatal in id's engine), where `<n>` is the computed entry count. Exactly 2048 entries loads.

A negative `dirlen` fails as PAK-2.4. The engine divides `dirlen` as an unsigned 32-bit value on the reference build, so any negative `dirlen` gives at least 33,554,432 entries; `dirlen` = -64 gives `has 67108863 files`. (A 64-bit build gets a different, also failing, result; the 32-bit answer is the one fixed here.)

A `dirlen` from 131,073 to 131,135 (2048 whole entries plus part of another) fails to load. id's code computes 2048 entries, passes the limit check and then reads `dirlen` bytes into a 131,072-byte stack array, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error because the C overflows its buffer.

A directory that does not lie wholly inside the file (a negative `dirofs`, or `dirofs + dirlen` past the end) fails to load. id's code does not check the seek or the length of the read and parses uninitialised stack memory, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
An entry's name is the bytes of its 56-byte field before the first NUL. Bytes after that NUL are ignored.

An entry whose 56-byte name field contains no NUL fails the load. id's `strcpy` runs on into `filepos`, `filelen` and the next entries, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error because no tool writes such a name and no single answer matches the C.

Names are kept as raw bytes: no case folding, no conversion between `/` and `\`, no trimming. `MAPS/E1M1.BSP` and `maps/e1m1.bsp` are two different names. An entry whose first name byte is NUL has the empty name.
Entries keep their directory order, and two entries may have the same name; loading neither merges nor rejects them.
`filepos` and `filelen` are not checked when the archive is loaded, so a bad range never stops an archive from loading or its directory from being listed (PAK-3.4 covers reading such an entry).
Looking up a name in an archive returns the first entry, in directory order, whose name is byte-for-byte equal to it. The comparison is case-sensitive and does not normalise separators.
An entry's contents are the `filelen` bytes starting at offset `filepos` of the PAK file. Entries may overlap each other, the header or the directory; nothing checks it.
An entry with `filelen` 0 has empty contents.

Reading an entry whose range does not lie wholly inside the file (a negative `filepos` or `filelen`, or `filepos + filelen` past the end) is an error. id's code either fails in `Hunk_AllocName` (`Hunk_Alloc: bad size` for `filelen` below -1), writes before its buffer (`filelen` = -1) or returns the short read's uninitialised bytes; this spec fixes the answer as an error. The entry is still listed (PAK-2.12).

The directory CRC is CRC-16 with polynomial 0x1021, not reflected, initial value 0xFFFF and no final XOR, computed over all `dirlen` bytes of the directory as they are in the file (before byte swapping, and including any partial entry from PAK-2.2). The CRC of an empty directory is 0xFFFF (65535).

An archive whose entry count is not 339 or whose directory CRC is not 32981 marks the game as modified. The check runs on every archive loaded, not only `pak0.pak`, and it never stops an archive from loading.

The rerelease's `pak0.pak` archives (in `id1`, `hipnotic`, `rogue`, `dopa`, `mg1` and the other game directories of FS-5.2) are PAK archives as described by PAK-1 to PAK-3, each with at most 2048 entries, and need no extension of the format. This statement rests on QuakeSpasm's evidence above; it is confirmed against a real install by the reader's acceptance test in [#42](https://github.com/quakecstudio/editor/issues/42), because no rerelease data is available to CI (LIC-4).
Every multi-byte integer and float in the file is little-endian. The engine converts with `LittleLong` and `LittleShort` after loading, so a big-endian host reads the same values.

The file starts with the 60-byte header (PROGS-2) at offset 0. Each of the six tables (statements, global definitions, field definitions, functions, strings, globals) is located only by its offset and count in the header; the engine does not require any order, alignment, gap or absence of overlap between them.

id's qcc writes the tables in this order, each directly after the previous one: header, strings, statements, functions, global definitions, field definitions, globals. It pads the string table with NUL bytes to a multiple of 4, so every table starts 4-byte aligned.
Bytes in the file that no table covers are ignored, except by the file CRC (PROGS-6.1).

The first record of the statements, functions, global definitions and field definitions tables, and the first byte of the string table, are reserved: qcc writes them as all zero bytes (`InitData` starts every count at 1). The engine does not check them.
The header is 15 consecutive `i32` fields, 60 bytes:

Every offset is measured from the first byte of the file. A table occupies `count * record size` bytes from its offset; for the string table the count is already in bytes and for the globals the record size is 4.
The fields are signed in id's struct. The engine never compares an offset or a count with the file size and never checks a sign; a reader's checks are in PROGS-15.
A file whose `version` is not 6 is rejected with `progs.dat has wrong version number (<version> should be 6)`.
A file whose `crc` is not 5927 is rejected with `progs.dat system vars have been modified, progdefs.h is out of date`.
The version is checked before the CRC: a file wrong in both reports the version.
A field definition whose `type` has bit 15 (`DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`) set is rejected with `PR_LoadProgs: pr_fielddefs[i].type & DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`. The same bit in a global definition is accepted (PROGS-9.3).

These three are the only checks the engine makes on a loaded file; it does not check offsets, counts, string references, opcodes or operands at load. A missing file is rejected with `PR_LoadProgs: couldn't load progs.dat`.

The header CRC identifies the system globals and fields a mod declares (PROGS-5), not the file: two different mods with the same system definitions carry the same value, 5927 for the definitions in id's `defs.qc`.

The CRC is the 16-bit, non-reflected CRC with polynomial 0x1021, initial value 0xFFFF and final XOR 0x0000 (CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE). Each byte updates it as `crc = (crc << 8) ^ table[(crc >> 8) ^ byte]`, truncated to 16 bits, where `table[i]` is the CRC of the single byte `i` with a zero initial value.
The CRC of no bytes is 0xFFFF (65535), and the CRC of the ASCII bytes `123456789` is 0x29B1.
The header `crc` is PROGS-4's CRC of exactly that text, with `\n` as one byte 0x0A. For `WinQuake/progdefs.q1` it is 5927.
qcc stores the CRC zero-extended from 16 bits, so the field is between 0 and 65535 in any file id's qcc writes.
While loading, the engine also computes PROGS-4's CRC over every byte of the file as stored, before any byte swapping, into `pr_crc`.
`pr_crc` is never checked. Its only use is the server info message, which prints it as `VERSION <version> SERVER (<pr_crc> CRC)`.
A statement is 8 bytes:

The operands are signed 16-bit: the bytes `ff ff` are -1, not 65535. Most opcodes use an operand as a global slot index; `OP_GOTO` uses `a`, and `OP_IF` and `OP_IFNOT` use `b`, as a jump relative to the statement. Their meaning per opcode is in `vm.md`.
Statement 0 is reserved (PROGS-1.5); a function's code starts at `first_statement` (PROGS-10) and the table has no other structure.
The engine does not check `op` or the operands at load. An opcode above `OP_BITOR` (65) fails only when executed, with `Bad opcode <op>`.
The vanilla opcodes are numbered from 0 in this order, 66 in all (0 to 65):
A definition is 8 bytes:
`ofs` is unsigned: a definition can name any slot from 0 to 65535, unlike a statement operand (PROGS-7.2).

In a global definition, `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL` marks a global that a saved game stores. qcc sets it on every global that has no initial value, is not a function or field, and is not a local or parameter. The engine strips the bit before using the type.
Several definitions can name the same slot: qcc gives a vector `v` the definitions `v` (vector) and `v_x` (float) at the same slot, and `v_y` and `v_z` at the next two.

For a field `.T name`, qcc writes a field definition with type `T` at the field's slot, and a global definition with type field (5) for a global slot whose value is that field slot index. A vector field also gets `name_x`, `name_y` and `name_z` field definitions and globals for its three slots.
Lookups by name compare bytes exactly (`strcmp`) and take the first matching definition in table order; lookups by slot take the first definition whose `ofs` matches.

qcc also writes global definitions for the parameters and locals of functions, without `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`, and one named `IMMEDIATE` for every constant slot it allocates (string, float and vector literals), so names in the table are not unique.
A function is 36 bytes:

A function with `first_statement` below zero is builtin number `-first_statement`; qcc writes `#25` as -25. The engine calls the builtin without reading `parm_start`, `locals`, `numparms` or `parm_size`.
A global of type function holds an index into this table, and index 0 is the null function: calling it fails with `NULL function`.
`parm_size` is eight single bytes and is not byte-swapped; entries at or past `numparms` are ignored (qcc writes them as 0).

`numparms` below zero copies no parameters; qcc writes -1 for a function declared with `...`. qcc does not limit the count to 8, but the engine reads only `parm_size[0..numparms)`, so a reader rejects more than 8 (PROGS-15.6).
The engine does not interpret `profile` at load; it adds one for every statement the function executes, starting from the stored value. qcc writes 0.

The string table is `numstrings` bytes holding NUL-terminated strings. A string reference (`s_name`, `s_file`, or the value of a string global) is a byte offset from the start of the table, and the string runs to the next NUL byte.
Offset 0 is the empty string: qcc writes a NUL as the first byte.

A reference may point into the middle of another string; the string is the bytes from that offset to the next NUL. qcc's `CopyString` appends every string it is given without looking for an earlier copy, so the same text can appear several times.
The bytes are uninterpreted: any value from 0x01 to 0xFF can be part of a string, including control characters and Quake's high-bit characters.
The table ends with zero to three NUL padding bytes from qcc (PROGS-1.3).

At run time a string value can also point outside the table, at strings the engine allocates (`ED_NewString`, `sv.name`); those values are still offsets from the start of the table and never appear in a file as written by qcc.

The globals are `numglobals` 4-byte slots holding the initial value of every global, constant and temporary. The engine executes in this memory directly, so the values in the file are the state before the first function runs.
A slot holds whichever type the code using it says (PROGS-17): the file does not tag slots with types, and only the definitions (PROGS-9) say what a named slot holds.
Slots 0 to 27 are the reserved return and parameter area (PROGS-18). qcc allocates every other global from slot 28 upward, so a file from qcc has at least 28 slots.
`entityfields` is the number of 4-byte field slots in every entity. The engine sizes each edict as `entityfields * 4` bytes of fields plus its own fixed header.
qcc counts one slot per non-vector field and three per vector field, in declaration order; a field's slot index is the count before it.
The engine does not check `entityfields` against the field definitions; [`edicts.md`](edicts.md) covers the system fields that must come first.
Loading a file that passes PROGS-3 yields every field of every record exactly as stored, after the little-endian conversion of PROGS-1.1; the loader changes no value.
Loading has no other effect on the file's contents: the tables keep their counts, order and duplicates, and the reserved first records stay as stored.
A file shorter than the 60-byte header is rejected.
A table whose offset or count is negative, or whose end (`offset + count * record size`) is past the end of the file, is rejected. The end is computed without overflow.
A string reference in a definition (`s_name`) or a function (`s_name`, `s_file`) that is negative or not less than `numstrings` is rejected.

A string reference whose bytes reach the end of the string table without a NUL is rejected. (id's engine would read on into the next table, or into the NUL that `COM_LoadFile` appends after the last byte of the file.)

A file is checked in this order and the first failure is reported: size, then version (PROGS-3.1), then header CRC (PROGS-3.2), then table bounds, then field definition flags (PROGS-3.4), then string references, then function parameter counts.
A function whose `numparms` is greater than 8 is rejected.

Statement opcodes and operands, function `first_statement`, `parm_start` and `locals`, definition `ofs`, and the values of globals are not checked at load, as in id's engine: what an out-of-range value does when executed is in `vm.md`.
A reader may skip the header CRC check (PROGS-3.2) when asked to, so the editor can open a mod whose system definitions differ from id's; the default is to check.

Within one step of PROGS-15.5 the first failure in this order is reported: table bounds in header order (statements, global definitions, field definitions, functions, strings, globals); field definitions in table order; string references of the global definitions, then of the field definitions, then of the functions, each in table order, with a function's `s_name` before its `s_file`; parameter counts in function order. id's engine has no such checks, so the order is ours; it follows the header and the loader's loops.
The type numbers used in definitions (PROGS-9.1) are:

The slot counts are id's `type_size` table. The engine computes the pointer's size as `sizeof(void *)/4`, which is 1 on the 32-bit x86 build id shipped and 2 on a 64-bit build; this spec fixes 1, the value of the shipped engine and of qcc's own table (`{1,1,1,3,1,1,1,1}`).

A definition type above 7 (after removing `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`) is not a vanilla type. id's engine has no check for it and prints such a value as `bad type <n>`; a reader keeps the number rather than rejecting the file.
QuakeC has no way to declare a pointer: `ev_pointer` values exist only at run time, made by `OP_ADDRESS`, and qcc writes no definition of type 7.
A slot is 4 bytes read either as an f32 or as an i32; the engine reinterprets the same bits (`eval_t` is a union) and never converts between them when copying.
A string value is an i32 byte offset from the start of the string table (PROGS-11); 0 is the empty string.
A float value is the f32 in the slot; a vector is three consecutive float slots, x first.

An entity value is an i32 byte offset from the start of the engine's edict array, which is the entity number times the engine's edict size, not the entity number; 0 is the world. The file never holds a non-zero entity value, since QuakeC cannot initialise one.
A field value is an i32 slot index into an entity's fields (PROGS-13), so `.origin_y` is one more than `.origin`.
A function value is an i32 index into the functions table (PROGS-10); 0 is the null function.
A pointer value is an i32 byte offset from the start of the engine's edict array to one field slot of one entity.

Slot 0 is `OFS_NULL`; slots 1 to 3 hold a function's return value (`OFS_RETURN`, three slots so a vector fits); slots 4 to 27 hold the eight call parameters, three slots each, parameter `n` at `4 + 3n`.
Slots 0 to 27 have no global definitions in a file from qcc, and the system globals start at slot 28, which is why `progdefs.h` opens with `int pad[28]` (PROGS-5.1).
A version 7 file has a 92-byte header: the 60 bytes of PROGS-2, then eight more 4-byte fields:
`secondaryversion` 0x021B1461 (`"1FTE" ^ "PROG"` as little-endian i32) means the 16-bit layout of PROGS-7 and PROGS-9; 0x65167402 (`"1FTE" ^ "32B "`) means the 32-bit layout of PROGS-20.
FTE also accepts version 7 with `secondaryversion` `"UH27"` or `"KKQW"`, or any other value (treated as KKQWSV's format). Those are other engines' layouts; a reader rejects them as unsupported.
In FTE's header the offsets and counts are unsigned, but they are bounded by the file size, so PROGS-15.2 applies unchanged.
In the 16-bit layout FTE declares statement operands unsigned (`dstatement16_t`), so in a version 7 file the bytes `ff ff` are operand 65535. This differs from PROGS-7.2, which holds for version 6.
In the 32-bit layout a statement is 16 bytes: `op`, `a`, `b` and `c`, each a u32, at offsets 0, 4, 8 and 12.
In the 32-bit layout a definition is 12 bytes: `type` u32 at 0, `ofs` u32 at 4 and `s_name` i32 at 8. `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL` is still bit 15 of `type`.
Functions, strings and globals keep the layout of PROGS-10 to PROGS-12.
When `ofslinenums` is not 0, it is the offset of `numstatements` i32 source line numbers, one per statement in statement order.
The bodyless function table is `numbodylessfuncs` NUL-terminated names stored one after another from `ofsbodylessfuncs`.

Bit `n` of `blockscompressed` set means a table is stored compressed: bit 0 statements, 1 global definitions, 2 field definitions, 3 functions, 4 strings, 5 globals, 6 line numbers, 7 types. A compressed table starts at its offset with an i32 compressed length followed by that many bytes of zlib data (`QC_decode` method 2).

A reader rejects a file with any `blockscompressed` bit set, as FTE does when built without zlib; reading compressed tables would add a decompressor for a mode that FTEQCC's default settings do not produce (`compressoutput` is zero-initialised in `qccmain.c`).
`ofsfiles` and the type table carry no information the engine needs to run the program; a reader keeps their offsets and counts and does not decode them.
The version 7 header is followed by the same six tables as version 6, and PROGS-15 applies to them; opcodes above 65 and type numbers above 7 are FTE extensions that the vanilla VM does not execute.
When `ofsfiles` is not 0, it is the offset of an i32 count followed by that many 144-byte embedded file records (`includeddatafile_t`, read by `PR_TestRecompile`):

When `ofs_types` is not 0, it is the offset of `numtypes` 28-byte type records (`typeinfo_t`): seven i32 fields `type`, `next`, `aux_type`, `num_parms`, `ofs`, `size` and `name`, the last a string reference. FTEQCC at the pinned commit never writes the table (`types` is always false in `WriteData`).

A version 7 file is checked in this order, and the first failure is reported: a size of at least 60 bytes (PROGS-15.1), the version, a size of at least 92 bytes, the header CRC (PROGS-3.2, which PROGS-15.8 may skip), `secondaryversion` (PROGS-19.3), `blockscompressed` (PROGS-21.4), the bounds of the six tables (PROGS-15.9), the bounds of the line number table when `ofslinenums` is not 0 (`numstatements` 4-byte entries, as PROGS-15.2), the bodyless function names (every name's NUL inside the file, and a table of no names still at an offset no greater than the file size), then the remaining steps of PROGS-15.5. The embedded files and the type table are not checked (PROGS-21.5). FTE's loader checks none of the bounds, so the order is ours.

When no non-empty table overlaps another or the header, a file the reader accepts and the writer writes back unchanged is the same byte for byte: the writer places the non-empty tables in the order the file had them, with the bytes before, between and after them that the file had (PROGS-1.4), and gives each empty table the offset the file stored.

Without a source layout (a file built in memory, or one with overlapping tables) the writer uses qcc's order (PROGS-1.3): header, strings, statements, functions, global definitions, field definitions, globals, then for version 7 the line numbers and the bodyless function names. It pads the string table with NUL bytes to a multiple of 4 and `numstrings` counts the padding. An empty table's offset is where it would start, except that an empty bodyless function table has offset 0.

The writer computes every count and offset in the header from the tables, `version` and `secondaryversion` from the format, and writes `blockscompressed` as 0; `crc`, `entityfields`, `ofsfiles`, `ofs_types` and `numtypes` are written as given. With a source layout, a table the source did not have, or had empty, and that now has records goes after the source's last byte. A version 7 file with no line number table has `ofslinenums` 0.

The writer rejects a value that does not fit its field, with a typed error and no output: in version 6 an opcode above 65535, an operand outside -32768 to 32767, or a definition type or `ofs` above 65535; in the 16-bit version 7 layout also an operand outside 0 to 65535; a count or offset above 2147483647; a line number table whose length is not the number of statements; a bodyless function name containing a NUL; version 7 parts in a version 6 file; and `ofsfiles` or `ofs_types` other than 0 without a source layout, since the bytes they point at would not be kept.
When the records given to the writer pass the checks of PROGS-15, reading the written file gives back every record exactly as given.
Opening a directory that holds `quakec.toml` opens that file (PRJ-2), and the directory is the project directory. Opening a `quakec.toml` file directly does the same.

Opening a directory without `quakec.toml` opens a bare project: its modules are the directory's `progs.src`, then its `csprogs.src` if there is one, then every source file either registers with `#pragma sourcefile` (PRJ-5.7), each read once in that order. A directory with neither `quakec.toml` nor `progs.src` is an error and opens nothing.
Opening any other file opens a bare project of that file and the source files it registers, with the file's directory as the project directory.

A bare project's name is the project directory's name (`project` when it has none), its mod name (PRJ-2.3) is that name when it is a valid mod name and `mod` otherwise, its dialect is `vanilla` and its target is `quake`. Each module's name is its source's path relative to the project directory, with `/` between components and without the extension when that is `.src`; its kind comes from its declared output (PRJ-3.3), and it has no defines and no include directories.

In a bare project, a file in source form (PRJ-4.1) that compiles no file but itself, declares no output and registers at least one source file is a list of programs, as FreeCS's top-level `progs.src` is: it is not a module, and the files it registers are.

`quakec.toml` holds an optional `[project]` table and one or more `[[module]]` tables with the keys above and no others. A key that is not listed, a value of the wrong type, a value outside its list, a file that is not valid TOML or a file with no `[[module]]` is an error that names the file, and the project does not open.
**Withdrawn** (P2-29, #407): it allowed only four targets. Replaced by PRJ-2.8 for `dialect` and PRJ-2.9 for `target`.
The mod name is the single directory name ADR-0008 puts the build output in. It is valid when it is not empty, is not `.` or `..`, and holds no `/`, `\` or `:`. An invalid `mod` is an error.
Module names are unique within a project; a repeated name is an error. A module without `name` is named after its kind.

`src`, `output` and each `include_dirs` entry are relative paths resolved against the project directory. An absolute `src`, `output` or include directory (one with a root, such as `/x`, or on Windows a drive), or an `output` with a `..` component, is an error, so build output never leaves the project.
Each `defines` entry is `NAME` or `NAME=VALUE`, where `NAME` is a QuakeC name (QC-3.1); `NAME` alone defines the macro with an empty body. Any other entry is an error.
A module's `#pragma sourcefile` lines (PRJ-5.7) add no modules: the modules of a project with `quakec.toml` are exactly those it declares.
`dialect` is one of `vanilla`, `fteqcc` and `gmqcc`. A module without its own `dialect` takes the project's.

`target` is one of `quake` (id's engine, which the preview host follows), `quakespasm`, `ironwail`, `vkquake`, `rerelease` (the 2021 KEX engine, a compile target only, ENG-8), `fte` and `dp`; each selects an engine of the engine-target database (`engine-targets.md`, ENGT-3.5 and ENGT-3.6). A module without its own `target` takes the project's.

A module is one program: a kind (`ssqc`, server QuakeC; `csqc`, client QuakeC; `menuqc`, menu QuakeC), a source (`src`), a dialect, a target, an output path and its file graph (PRJ-6). Modules are separate programs, each with its own symbol table (LANG-3): a macro, include directory or `#pragma once` of one module does not carry into another.

A module's output path is its `output` when `quakec.toml` gives one, and otherwise `build/<mod>/<file>` with the file name of its kind: `PRJ_SSQC_OUTPUT`, `PRJ_CSQC_OUTPUT` or `PRJ_MENUQC_OUTPUT`. The output the `progs.src` itself declares (PRJ-4.3, PRJ-5.6) is kept as the module's declared output and does not change where the IDE writes (ADR-0008: nothing is written outside the project).

In a bare project a module's kind is `csqc` when the file name of its declared output is `csprogs.dat`, `menuqc` when it is `menu.dat`, compared without regard to ASCII case, and `ssqc` otherwise, including when it declares none.

A module's source is read in list form or source form, decided by its first token as QC-23.2 splits tokens, with `/* */` comments also skipped: source form when the first token starts with `#`, list form otherwise. The file's extension does not matter.

In list form the tokens are split as QC-23.2 says, and in addition `/* */` comments are skipped and a line whose first non-blank byte is `#` followed by a name is a directive (PRJ-5), not tokens. Neither changes a list id's `qcc` accepts: no such list has a `/*` or a line starting `#` and a name, because each would be a file name it cannot open.

In list form the first token is the declared output, resolved against the directory of the `progs.src`, and every later token is a source file, resolved against the same directory and compiled in the order listed (QC-23.3). The `progs.src` itself is not compiled. A list with no token is error `E0401` (QCD-5.1).

In source form the file is itself the first file compiled: its text is QuakeC, and the files it brings in with `#include` and `#includelist` are compiled where they appear. It declares its output with `#output` or `#pragma progs_dat` (PRJ-5.6), or not at all.
A module's source that cannot be read is error `E0402` (QCD-5.2) and the module has no files.

Under the FTEQCC and GMQCC dialects a module's source is read as the text FTEQCC's `QCC_LoadFile` gives it (`dialect-fteqcc.md` FTEF-14.54): FTEQCC's `QCC_main` loads it with `if (QCC_LoadFile (qccmprogsdat, (void *)&qccmsrc) == -1)` before `pr_file_p = QCC_COM_Parse(qccmsrc);` reads its first word and `if (*qcc_token == '#')` picks the source form (`qccmain.c`, fte-team/fteqw@`f937b9d88f71fc4429db5fe56c6a98d922711b2e`). So a source that starts with a UTF-16 or UTF-32 byte order mark is decoded before PRJ-4.1 tells its form and before a list's words are read, a UTF-8 mark is skipped once, and each NUL byte is a space that splits two words; the source form is then read as PRJ-5.13 says. The graph cases of the directive family of `cargo xtask oracles builtins` with a `progs.src` of their own (`progs_cases` in `xtask/src/oracles/builtins/directives.rs`) hold each form in each wide encoding and with NULs and marks, and the graph lists the file that binds `f` exactly when the pinned FTEQCC binds it. The GMQCC dialect reads its source so too, as it reads every file with FTEQCC's reader (PRJ-5.15): GMQCC's own reading is not quoted here and waits for its dialect profile, as PRJ-5.15 says. Under the vanilla dialect the source is read as PRJ-4.7 says.

Under the vanilla dialect a module's form is told from, and a list's words are read from, its bytes past a UTF-8 byte order mark (PRJ-5.1) up to the NUL byte where id's `qcc` ends its list (QC-23.7): the first NUL between words, or that ends a word or a `//` comment. A quoted word runs on past a NUL in it, here to its closing quote or its line's end, and names the file of its text up to that NUL. So `progs.dat`, a NUL and `a.qc` list no file, and a source that starts with a NUL is a list with no token, error `E0401`. A source in source form is then read as its bytes (PRJ-5.1), as before. The vanilla graph cases of the directive family of `cargo xtask oracles builtins` with a `progs.src` of their own (`VANILLA_PROGS` in `xtask/src/oracles/builtins/directives.rs`) hold a NUL between words, in and after a word, in a `//` comment and in a quoted word, and the graph lists the file that binds `f` exactly when the pinned id `qcc` binds it.

Under the FTEQCC and GMQCC dialects a module's source whose text, as PRJ-4.6 gives it, starts with the two bytes `#!` has its first line passed over before PRJ-4.1 tells its form, before a list's words are read and before the source form is read as PRJ-5.13 says and as the preprocessor reads it: FTEQCC's `QCC_main` (`qccmain.c`, fte-team/fteqw@`f937b9d88f71fc4429db5fe56c6a98d922711b2e`) runs `if (qccmsrc[0] == '#' && qccmsrc[1] == '!') qccmsrc = strchr(qccmsrc, '\n');` ("ignore the first line if it starts with a #! for unix scripts") after `QCC_LoadFile` and before `pr_file_p = QCC_COM_Parse(qccmsrc);`. The line is passed over whatever it holds: a `\` at its end joins nothing to the next line, and a `/*` or `"` in it opens nothing. The test is of the first two bytes of that text, so it holds after a UTF-8 mark that is skipped and in a decoded UTF-16 or UTF-32 source, and not after a blank or a NUL. A source of one such line with no line feed is all passed over, since `QCC_LoadFile` writes a line feed after the text, and is a list with no token, error `E0401` (PRJ-4.3), as an empty source is; the pinned FTEQCC reads either with an empty output name and writes nothing ("nothing to write"), which the graph does not follow. The line keeps its place, so the lines after it keep their numbers. The vanilla dialect reads a `#!` line as PRJ-4.1 and PRJ-4.7 say. The graph cases of the directive family of `cargo xtask oracles builtins` with a `progs.src` of their own hold a `#!` first line before a list and before a source form, after a UTF-8 mark and in each wide encoding, and with a `\`, a `/*` and a `"` in it, and the graph lists the file that binds `f` exactly when the pinned FTEQCC binds it. The GMQCC dialect reads its source so too, as PRJ-4.6 says.

A directive is a line, outside any `/* */` comment, whose first non-blank byte is `#` followed, after optional blanks, by a name (QC-9.1). A line ending in `\` continues on the next line. Directive names are compared exactly; pragma names (PRJ-5.6 to PRJ-5.9) without regard to ASCII case. Text in string literals and comments never starts a directive or a comment. A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of a file is skipped, as FTEQCC's `QCC_LoadFile` (`qcc_cmdlib.c`) skips it.

`#include "path"` and `#include <path>` compile the named file at that point. The path is resolved against the directory of the file holding the directive, then against each include directory in order (the module's `include_dirs`, then those added by `#pragma includedir`); the first that names a readable file is used. None is error `E0111` (QCD-8.4), and the line is skipped.

`#includelist` starts a list that runs to a line `#endlist`. Each word of the lines between is a file, found as `#include` finds one and compiled in order. Words are split at blanks and at `,`, `;`, `(`, `)` and `]`, `//` ends the line, a pair of `"` around a word is removed, and directive lines inside the list are followed (so `#ifdef` can skip entries). A word that names no readable file is error `E0402` (QCD-5.2). A file that ends inside a list is error `E0406` (QCD-5.6), and the list ends there.

`#define NAME text` and `#undef NAME` define and remove macros for the conditionals; a function-like `#define` defines its name. Macros from a module's `defines` are defined first, and macros run on across the files of the module in compilation order (QC-9.8).

`#ifdef NAME`, `#ifndef NAME`, `#if expr`, `#elif expr`, `#elifdef NAME`, `#elifndef NAME`, `#else` and `#endif` skip lines as in C (FTEQCC reads the last two `#elif` forms in `QCC_PR_FalsePreProcessorIf`): in a skipped block only these directives are read, for nesting, and comments are not tracked. An `#if` or `#elif` expression is made of decimal integers, names, `defined NAME`, `defined(NAME)`, parentheses, `!`, `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `&&` and `||` with C's precedence. A name's value is its macro's text read as a decimal integer, and 0 when the macro is undefined or its text is not a number. An expression that does not parse is false. A block is closed in the file that opens it (QC-9.12); an `#else`, `#elif` or `#endif` without a block is skipped.
`#output "path"` and `#pragma progs_dat "path"` declare the module's output, resolved against the directory of the file holding them; a later one replaces an earlier one.
`#pragma sourcefile a b ...` registers each token (QC-23.2 rules) as another program's source, resolved against the directory of the module's source. A file registered twice is one program.
`#pragma includedir "path"` adds an include directory, resolved against the directory of the file holding it, after the ones already in use, for the rest of the module.
`#pragma once` marks the file holding it: a later `#include`, `#includelist` entry or list entry naming it again compiles nothing.

An `#if` or `#elif` expression whose value stands inside more than 63 parentheses and `!`s together is false, as one that does not parse is: the reader nests at most `MAX_DEPTH` = 64 levels (`qc-preproc`'s `cond.rs`), the value itself one, so no input can exhaust its stack. `&&`, `||` and the comparisons chain without nesting. Under an FTEQCC profile the limit is FTEF-14.12's.

Under the FTEQCC dialect (GMQCC's is PRJ-5.12) the file being compiled, FTEQCC's `compilingfile`, stands where PRJ-5.2, PRJ-5.3, PRJ-5.8 and PRJ-5.9 say the file holding the directive: an `#include` and an `#includelist` entry are resolved against its directory (`QCC_FindBestInclude(msg, compilingfile, ...)`, `dialect-fteqcc.md` FTEF-14.40), a `#pragma includedir` path is joined to it, and `#pragma once` marks it. The file being compiled is the source of the source form, an entry of a list-form `progs.src` or of an `#includelist`, never an `#include`d file, which is read for the file that includes it. So with `progs.src` listing `src/a.qc`, which includes `x/b.qh`, which includes `c.qh`, the graph reads `src/c.qh`, as the pinned FTEQCC does.

Under the GMQCC dialect an `#include` is found beside the file holding it, then beside the file being compiled, then in the module's include directories (PRJ-5.2), which GMQCC itself has none of: its `ftepp_include_find` tries `ftepp_include_find_path(file, ftepp->includename)` and then `ftepp_include_find_path(file, ftepp->itemname)`, and `ftepp_directive_include` sets `ftepp->includename = filename;` to the included file while it reads it (graphitemaster/gmqcc@b2a319efb41069b9a250e76991dbe505ff8d030d, `ftepp.cpp`). GMQCC's preprocessor has no `#includelist` and passes `#pragma` lines to its compiler (`ftepp_out(ftepp, "#", false);`), so it is silent on them; this dialect keeps PRJ-5.3, PRJ-5.8 and PRJ-5.9 for an `#includelist` entry, `#pragma includedir` and `#pragma once`, the file holding the directive, as the C preprocessor Xonotic is read with marks the header that holds `#pragma once`, and the preprocessor does the same. So with `progs.src` listing `src/a.qc`, which includes `x/b.qh`, which includes `c.qh`, the graph reads `src/x/c.qh`, and `src/c.qh` when that is missing. Xonotic, which the C preprocessor reads before GMQCC compiles it, relies on the first of these.

Under the FTEQCC dialect the graph reads each QuakeC file, the source of the source form, each list entry, each `#includelist` entry and each `#include`d file, with the preprocessor's directive reader (`qc_preproc::FteFileReader`) in place of the lines of PRJ-5.1 and the reading of PRJ-5.3 to PRJ-5.5, as FTEQCC's `QCC_PR_Precompiler` reads it (`engine/qclib/qcc_pr_lex.c`, fte-team/fteqw@`f937b9d88f71fc4429db5fe56c6a98d922711b2e`; `dialect-fteqcc.md` FTEF-14.33 to FTEF-14.48, FTEF-14.52). A directive is at a `#` that `QCC_PR_NewLine` reaches, at a compiled file's start after spaces and tabs and at an included file's first byte (FTEF-14.52), its name matched by its first bytes, so `#defined N 1` defines `N` and `#iffy` opens no block; its line ends where `QCC_PR_SkipToEndOfLine` ends it (FTEF-14.35), so after `#undef N // c \` the next line, an `#include` too, is the directive's; `#if` and `#elif` read as FTEF-14.33 says; a side that is not taken is skipped by `QCC_PR_FalsePreProcessorIf` (FTEF-14.37), whose one count of open sides runs from file to file, so a side an included file leaves open is closed, or ended by an `#else`, in the file that included it, and QC-9.12 does not hold; `#eof` and `#package` end the file, and `#pragma DONT_COMPILE_THIS_FILE` passes over the rest of it with the directives at its lines' starts still run (FTEF-14.39, FTEF-14.44); an `#includelist`'s words, and the directives on its lines, are read as FTEF-14.41 says, so a word in quotes names a file with the quotes in its name; and `FTEQCC` and `__FTEQCC__` are defined before the module's `defines` (FTEF-14.48). Between directives the code is read as the preprocessor reads it, a token of its lexer at a time, a `#` token that starts a line as FTEF-14.52 says being a directive's, so no string, raw string `R"d(...)d"`, character constant or comment starts one, and the graph meets a directive where the preprocessor does. A list-form `progs.src` is still read as PRJ-5.1 and QC-23 say, in the text PRJ-4.6 gives. So the graph lists the files the pinned FTEQCC compiles for a program that brings a file in, by an `#include` or an `#includelist`, after or around each directive form of FTEF-14.35 to FTEF-14.44 and FTEF-14.52: the graph cases of the directive family of `cargo xtask oracles builtins`, whose one file that binds `f` FTEQCC binds it from exactly when the graph lists it.

Deliberate divergences of PRJ-5.13, as the graph expands no macro: a directive a macro's body or arguments hold is run where it stands in the file's text, not where the expansion is read (FTEF-14.45, FTEF-14.46); an `#include` in the text `#pragma DONT_COMPILE_THIS_FILE` passes over, in an `#includelist` there too, brings in no file and runs none of its directives, where FTEQCC passes over that file's text too, running its directives, so a macro it defines or a list it holds is FTEQCC's and not the graph's; the conditionals of a list-form `progs.src` are its own, as PRJ-5.5 and QC-9.12 say, where FTEQCC's one count of open sides runs through it too; an `#include` among an `#includelist`'s lines brings its file in as an `#include`, where FTEQCC reads that file's words as the list's (FTEF-14.47); a program FTEQCC stops at an error, such as an `#error` or "unexpected tokens at end of line", is read on to its end; and an `#includelist` or `DONT_COMPILE_THIS_FILE` met while 64 others are open in one file ends that file, as the preprocessor's bound on nested directives does (FTEF-14.47), so that no file exhausts the graph's memory.

Under the GMQCC dialect the graph reads each QuakeC file as PRJ-5.13 and PRJ-5.14 say, with the preprocessor's directive reader, which the preprocessor reads a GMQCC file with too, so the two meet the same directives and list the same files; PRJ-5.12 still says where an `#include`, an `#includelist` entry, `#pragma includedir` and `#pragma once` are resolved. Neither defines `FTEQCC` or `__FTEQCC__`: GMQCC's `ftepp_create` defines `GMQCC` and, by the standard chosen, `__STD_FTEQCC__`, `__STD_GMQCC__`, `__STD_QCCX__` or `__STD_QCC__`, never `FTEQCC` (`ftepp_add_define(ftepp, nullptr, "GMQCC");`, graphitemaster/gmqcc@b2a319efb41069b9a250e76991dbe505ff8d030d, `ftepp.cpp`), and the C preprocessor Xonotic is read with (`CPP := cc -xc -E`, Xonotic's `qcsrc/Makefile`) defines neither, so `#ifdef FTEQCC` is false and Xonotic's `server/progs.inc` skips its `#pragma target`. A `\` that ends a directive's `//` comment carries the next line, an `#include` too, into the directive (FTEF-14.35), as the C preprocessor does, whose line splicing comes before comments are replaced ("Whenever backslash appears at the end of a line (immediately followed by the newline character), both backslash and newline are deleted", phase 2, before phase 3's "Each comment is replaced by one space character", https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/language/translation_phases, read 2026-10-21). GMQCC's own lexer ends a `//` comment at its line break (`while (ch != EOF && ch != '\n')`, `lex_skipwhite`, `lexer.cpp` at the same commit), so the comment does not carry the next line: a deliberate divergence from `ftepp`, since Xonotic, the GMQCC corpus, is built with the C preprocessor. The rest of the reading is FTEQCC's too, where `ftepp` and the C preprocessor read otherwise: a `//` comment of code that ends in a `\` carries nothing, so an `#include` on the next line is read (FTEF-14.52), where the C preprocessor's splicing hides it; directive names match by their first bytes (`#defined Q 1` defines `Q`); and an `#include`d file's first line is a directive's only at its first byte. The GMQCC dialect's own reading waits for its dialect profile. GMQCC's own macros are a module's `defines` (PRJ-5.4), as Xonotic's `quakec.toml` gives `GMQCC`.

A module's file graph is the list of files the module compiles, in compilation order: each file appears where it starts to be read, before the files it brings in. Each entry records its path, how it came in (the source-form root, a list entry, an `#includelist` entry or an `#include`) and the entry of the file that brought it in.
A file brought in more than once is compiled, and appears, each time, except as PRJ-5.9 says. Files in the source directory that nothing brings in are not part of the module (QC-23.6).

A file that brings in a file already being read, directly or through others, reads it again from the start, as FTEQCC (`QCC_Include` has no guard) and the C preprocessor Xonotic builds with do; `#pragma once` is how such a file stops it. Bringing in a file while `PRJ_MAX_DEPTH` files are being read is error `E0408` (QCD-5.8), and that file is skipped. The vanilla preprocessor is stricter (QC-9.11); that is a dialect difference, and the graph follows the compilers that accept such projects.
A graph holds at most `PRJ_MAX_FILES` entries. Bringing in one more is error `E0407` (QCD-5.7), and the graph stops there.
Every diagnostic names the file and the 1-based line of the directive or list entry that raised it, or line 0 when it is about the whole source: one that cannot be read or has no token.

A name that brings a file into the graph (a list entry, PRJ-4.3; an `#include`, PRJ-5.2; an `#includelist` entry, PRJ-5.3), once resolved, is opened as the host file system opens that path, as both compilers do: exactly where the file system matches case, and ignoring case where it does not. The entry's path is the resolved name in the name's own case. So a name that differs in case from its file opens on macOS and Windows and is `E0402` or `E0111` on Linux, where FTEQCC and id's `qcc` fail too.

When a name opens a file, each path component the name spells (the components it adds to the directory it was resolved against, once `.` and `..` are folded away) is compared with the entry the directory holding it stores. When an entry with exactly that name exists it matches; otherwise the entry whose name differs only in case is the stored one. If any component differs, the graph reports warning `W0402` (QCD-7.16) at the line of the entry or directive, naming the name and the stored spelling of the components it spells, once per entry brought in. The stored names are read from the directory, not inferred from whether the file opened, so the warning is the same on every OS where the file opens: a project that would fail on a case-sensitive file system says so on macOS and Windows too. The directory the name was resolved against is not compared.

Names that bring no file into the graph are opened as PRJ-7.1 says and not compared: a module's `src`, the `progs.src` and `csprogs.src` of PRJ-1.2, `#pragma sourcefile` entries, include directories and declared outputs.

A sprite starts with a 36-byte header: `ident`, `version`, `type` as signed 32-bit integers, `boundingradius` as a float, `width`, `height` and `numframes` as signed 32-bit integers, `beamlength` as a float and `synctype` as a signed 32-bit integer.
A sprite's first four bytes are `IDSP` (0x49 0x44 0x53 0x50). A file that does not start with them is not a sprite: the engine loads it as another kind of model, and the sprite reader rejects it.
`version` must be 1; any other value fails with the error `<name> has wrong version number (<version> should be 1)` (fatal in id's engine).
`numframes` must be at least 1; 0 or a negative value fails with the error `Mod_LoadSpriteModel: Invalid # of frames: <numframes>` (fatal in id's engine).

`type`, `boundingradius`, `width`, `height`, `beamlength` and `synctype` are not checked when the sprite loads. A `type` other than 0 to 4 loads and fails only when the sprite is drawn (`R_DrawSprite: Bad sprite type <type>` in `WinQuake/r_sprite.c`, `R_DrawSprite`); the frames are not checked against `width` and `height`.
A file shorter than the 36-byte header fails to load. id's code reads the header from the loaded buffer without checking its length, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

The model's bounds are `mins = (-width / 2, -width / 2, -height / 2)` and `maxs = (width / 2, width / 2, height / 2)` with C integer division, which truncates toward zero, so a width of 33 gives -16 and 16. The negation comes before the division and wraps as on x86, so a width of -2147483648 gives -1073741824 for both.

After the header come `numframes` frame entries, each starting with a 32-bit frame type. A type of 0 (`SPR_SINGLE`) is followed by one frame; any other value, not only 1 (`SPR_GROUP`), is followed by a frame group.

A frame is a 16-byte `dspriteframe_t` (`origin[0]`, `origin[1]`, `width`, `height`) followed by `width * height` bytes of palette indices, row by row from the top left. The next entry starts right after the pixels.
A frame's extents are `up = origin[1]`, `down = origin[1] - height`, `left = origin[0]` and `right = width + origin[0]`, computed in 32-bit integers that wrap as on x86.

A frame with a negative `width` or `height`, whose `width * height` does not fit in a 32-bit signed integer, or whose header or pixels run past the end of the file, fails to load. id's code copies `width * height` bytes without checking them, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
A frame group is a 32-bit `numframes`, then `numframes` float intervals, then `numframes` frames as in SPR-2.2, with no frame type before each.
Every interval must be greater than 0; one that is 0 or less fails with the error `Mod_LoadSpriteGroup: interval<=0` (fatal in id's engine). The test is `interval <= 0.0`, so a NaN interval loads.

A frame group's `numframes` must be at least 1. id's code loads a group of 0 frames, and `R_GetSpriteframe` then reads the interval before the group's array, which is undefined; a negative count fails in id's `Hunk_AllocName`. This spec fixes both as an error.
An interval or frame of a group that runs past the end of the file fails to load, as in SPR-2.4.
Bytes after the last frame entry are ignored.
A trace is one header (TRACE-2) followed by zero or more records (TRACE-4), in the order the events they describe happened. It has no end marker: it ends after its last complete record.
The binary form (TRACE-5) and the JSON form (TRACE-6) hold the same information. Decoding either form and encoding the result in the other, then decoding that, gives back the same header and records.

The header is written after the progs is loaded (its globals hold the values the file gives them) and before the first run. Every run the host starts after that is traced, including runs nested inside builtins (VM-18).

Globals are named by slot number, edicts by edict number (0 is the world) and entity fields by field slot number (PROGS-13), never by an address or an entity value, so the names do not depend on how a VM lays out its memory. Values are the raw 32-bit patterns of the slots (PROGS-17.1), written exactly, NaN payloads included.

The header holds the format version and five numbers: `progs_crc`, the CRC of the whole progs.dat file (PROGS-6.1, id's `pr_crc`), so a reader can check that two traces ran the same file; `edict_size`, the bytes between the entity values of consecutive edicts in this VM (id's `pr_edict_size`); `field_offset`, the bytes from an entity value to the pointer value of its field slot 0; `entityfields`, the number of field slots per edict (the progs header's `entityfields`); and `numstrings`, the size of the loaded string table in bytes.
The version is `TRACE_VERSION`. A reader rejects any other version: a change to the format that an old reader would misread is a new version.

`edict_size` is at least 1, `progs_crc` fits in 16 bits, and the fields fit inside an edict: `field_offset + 4 * entityfields` is at most `edict_size`, computed without overflow. A reader rejects a header that breaks any of these, and an emitter cannot write one.

A change set lists every global slot and every entity field slot whose 32-bit pattern, at the moment the record is written, differs from its pattern when the previous change-carrying record was written, or, for the first one, when the header was written. The patterns are compared as bits, so `-0.0` differs from `0.0` and a NaN equals itself only when its bits do.
Each slot appears at most once, with its value at the moment the record is written. A slot that changed and then changed back to its earlier pattern is not listed.
Global changes are in ascending order of slot. Field changes are in ascending order of edict number, and of field slot within one edict.

The globals compared are slots 0 to `numglobals - 1`. The fields compared are slots 0 to `entityfields - 1` of every edict the VM has in use (in id's engine edicts 0 to `sv.num_edicts - 1`), free or not. An edict that was not in use at the previous change-carrying record is compared against all-zero fields, so a newly allocated edict lists only its non-zero fields.

Only the globals and the fields are compared. The call stack, the local stack, the runaway counter, `pr_argc` and whether an edict is free are not in a change set; the differences they make show up in later globals and fields, or in the records' order.

A run record is written when the host or a builtin calls `PR_ExecuteProgram`, before any of the checks of VM-2. It holds the function index as passed, a signed 32-bit number, and a change set: for a run started by the host, the host's own changes since the previous record (setting `self` and `time`, spawning edicts); for a nested run, what the builtin changed before starting it.

A step record is written when a statement finishes without an error. It holds the index of the function that was current when the statement became current (VM-3.1), before any call or return the statement makes; the statement's index; its opcode as the statement stores it (PROGS-7.1); the builtin number when there is one (TRACE-4.3); and a change set.

A step record has a builtin number exactly when its statement is a `CALL0` to `CALL8` that called a builtin (VM-14.4): the number `-first_statement` of the function it called. The step's change set includes what the builtin wrote, `OFS_RETURN` among it.

When a builtin starts nested runs, each run's records (its run record, its statements' records and its exit or error record) are written while the builtin is running, so they come before the step record of the `CALL` that called the builtin. That step record's change set holds what the builtin changed after the last nested run returned.

An exit record is written when `PR_ExecuteProgram` returns to its caller (VM-16.4). It holds only a change set, which is normally empty: the `DONE` or `RETURN` that ended the run has its own step record.

An error record is written instead of a step record when a runtime error ends the run (VM-19.1, VM-19.7), and also for the errors a run raises before its first statement (VM-2.1, VM-2.2, VM-2.4). It holds a function index, a statement index, the message and a change set (VM-19.5 says what a failed statement may already have written).

For an error raised by a statement, an error record's function and statement are the ones `PR_RunError` prints (VM-19.1): the current function and statement, so for `runaway loop error` the statement before the one that was not run. For an error raised before a run's first statement (VM-2.1, VM-2.2, VM-2.4), the function is the index the run was given and the statement is -1.

An error record's message is the error's text as [`vm.md`](vm.md) gives it, without a trailing newline (`Bad opcode 70`, `NULL function`); for the errors of VM-19.7, which have no message in id's code, it is the implementation's own text. It contains no NUL byte.
After an error record, no record follows for any run that was active when the error happened (VM-19.2). The host may then start a new run, which begins with its own run record.

A string record is written whenever the VM makes a string value that lies outside the string table (PROGS-11.6) name some text: when a builtin or the host allocates an engine string, and whenever the text at such a value changes (id's `ftos`, `vtos` and `etos` all write `pr_string_temp` in `WinQuake/pr_cmds.c`). It holds the 32-bit string value and the text up to, not including, its NUL. It is written before the change-carrying record whose change set first shows the value, and it carries no change set: it does not reset what the next change set compares against (TRACE-3.1).

Numbers are written in three ways. A *word* is 4 bytes, little-endian. A *uvar* is an unsigned 32-bit number in LEB128: 7 bits per byte, least significant group first, the high bit set on every byte but the last. A *svar* is a signed 32-bit number `n` written as the uvar of its zigzag form, `(n << 1) ^ (n >> 31)` with an arithmetic shift, so 0, -1, 1, -2 become 0, 1, 2, 3.

A uvar is at most 5 bytes and uses the fewest bytes that hold its value: a reader rejects a uvar that runs past 5 bytes, one whose fifth byte is above 0x0F (the value would not fit in 32 bits), and one with more than one byte whose last byte is 0x00.
*Text* is a uvar byte count followed by that many bytes, none of them NUL.
The header is 28 bytes: the magic `QCTR` (0x51 0x43 0x54 0x52), then six words: the version, `progs_crc`, `edict_size`, `field_offset`, `entityfields` and `numstrings`.

A change set is a uvar count of global changes, each a uvar slot and a word holding the slot's bits, then a uvar count of field changes, each a uvar edict number, a uvar field slot and a word holding the bits.
Each record is a tag byte followed by its fields, in this order:

A reader rejects a stream that is shorter than the header or has the wrong magic, a record that ends before its last field, an unknown tag, a builtin flag byte other than 0x00 or 0x01, an opcode above 65535, and a change set that breaks the order of TRACE-3.3 or lists a slot twice. Because every value has exactly one encoding, encoding what a reader accepted gives back the same bytes.
The JSON form is JSON Lines: one JSON object per line, each line ended by a line feed (0x0A), the header on the first line and one record on each line after it. There are no blank lines.
The header is `{"trace":"qc-trace","version":1,"progs_crc":N,"edict_size":N,"field_offset":N,"entityfields":N,"numstrings":N}`.

A record's `t` key names it: `run`, `step`, `exit`, `error` or `string`. A run has `function`; a step has `function`, `statement`, `opcode` and, only when it has one, `builtin`; an error has `function`, `statement` and `message`; a string has `value` and `text`. Every change-carrying record also has `globals`, an array of `[slot, bits]`, and `fields`, an array of `[edict, field, bits]`, each empty when there are no changes. Numbers are JSON integers.
A 32-bit pattern (`bits`, and a string record's `value`) is a JSON string of exactly 8 lowercase hexadecimal digits: `"3f800000"` is 1.0.

Text (`message`, `text`) is a JSON string in which each byte from 0x20 to 0x7E other than the backslash stands for itself, and every other byte, the backslash included, is the four characters `\x` and two lowercase hexadecimal digits. In the JSON source the backslash is itself escaped, so the text `a\b` followed by a line feed is `"a\\x5cb\\x0a"`.

A writer puts the keys in the order TRACE-6.2 and TRACE-6.3 list them (`t` first), with no whitespace, and escapes text with JSON's own escapes only where RFC 8259 requires them (`\"` and `\\`). A reader accepts any key order and any JSON whitespace within a line, and rejects a missing key, an unknown key, a value of the wrong JSON type, a number out of range for its field, bits or text not written as TRACE-6.4 and TRACE-6.5 say, and the violations of TRACE-2.3 and TRACE-5.7 that the JSON form can express.
A 32-bit pattern read as a signed number `v` is the entity value of edict `n` when `v` is `n * edict_size` exactly, with `n` 0 or more. 0 is the world in every trace.
A pattern `v` is the pointer to field slot `f` of edict `n` when `v` is `n * edict_size + field_offset + 4 * f` exactly, with `n` 0 or more and `f` from 0 to `entityfields - 1`.

A string value `v` from 0 to `numstrings - 1` is an offset into the string table, the same in every trace of one progs. Any other string value names the text of the latest string record for `v` before the point being read, and no text if there is none.

The VM state is the globals (PROGS-12), the edicts, a call stack of frames (each the statement to return to and the function it belongs to), the call depth, a local stack of `LIMIT_LOCALSTACK_SIZE` slots and the number of them in use, the current function, the current statement and the argument count of the last call (`pr_argc`). All of it persists from one `PR_ExecuteProgram` call to the next; only the runaway counter belongs to one call (VM-2.3).
Execution reads the statements and functions tables and never writes them, except each function's `profile` counter (VM-3.1).

Each opcode uses its operands as VM-3.6 says. An operand used as a global slot names one slot for a scalar and the three slots `n`, `n+1`, `n+2` for a vector; an opcode reads and writes only the slots its section names. An operand the opcode does not use is ignored, whatever its value.

id's VM checks no operand: `PARANOID` is commented out in `quakedef.h`, so a global slot outside `0` to `numglobals - 1` is read or written outside the globals, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: a statement that would read or write a global slot outside that range fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7) before it changes any global or field. It is a deliberate divergence; qcc never writes such an operand.

A function index of 0, or not less than `numfunctions`, fails with `PR_ExecuteProgram: NULL function`. This error goes straight to `Host_Error`, not through `PR_RunError`: no statement or stack trace is printed, the call depth is not reset, and when the global `self` is not 0 the engine prints that entity first.

A negative function index passes id's test (`!fnum || fnum >= numfunctions`) and reads before the start of the functions table, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: it fails as VM-2.1 does.

A run sets its own runaway counter to `LIMIT_RUNAWAY` (LIMIT-4.1), clears the statement trace flag (`pr_trace`, set by the `traceon` builtin), records the current call depth as its exit depth, and enters the function as VM-15 says. It returns to its caller when a return brings the call depth back to the exit depth (VM-16.4).

A builtin (`first_statement` below 0) passed to `PR_ExecuteProgram` is entered as if it were a QC function, and execution starts at the negative statement index `first_statement`, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: it fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7) before any statement runs. The engine never does this with id's progs.

Each step of the loop moves to the next statement (the current one plus one), decrements the runaway counter and, if it reaches 0, fails with `runaway loop error` without executing the statement (LIMIT-4.1). Otherwise it adds one to the current function's `profile`, makes the statement current and executes it.

Nothing marks the end of a function: execution runs on into the next statement in the table, whichever function it belongs to, until a `DONE` or `RETURN` (VM-16), a jump (VM-13) or a call (VM-14) moves it.

Reaching a statement index outside `0` to `numstatements - 1` (by running past the last statement, by a jump, or through a function's `first_statement`) reads outside the statements table, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: it fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7) before the statement executes.
An opcode above 65 fails with `Bad opcode <op>`, the opcode printed as an unsigned decimal number (PROGS-7.4). The step has already counted against the runaway counter and `profile`.
Statement 0 is reserved and all zero (PROGS-1.5), so executing it is `DONE 0 0 0`: a jump to statement 0, or a function whose `first_statement` is 0 (LIMIT-5.2), returns at once.
The operands of each opcode are:

`c = a + b`, `a - b`, `a * b` or `a / b` in IEEE 754 single precision with round-to-nearest-even, the result rounded to f32 once. Subnormal operands and results are kept, not flushed to zero, and signed zeros follow IEEE 754 (`-0 - +0` is `-0`).

No arithmetic opcode fails. Overflow gives an infinity; a non-zero finite value divided by zero gives an infinity whose sign is the exclusive or of the operands' signs (so `1 / -0` is `-inf`); `0 / 0`, `inf - inf`, `inf / inf` and `0 * inf` give a NaN; and any NaN operand gives a NaN.

The sign and payload of a NaN that an operation produces are not specified: C leaves them to the CPU, and they differ between hosts (x86 produces 0xFFC00000 for `0 / 0`, ARM 0x7FC00000). An implementation may produce any NaN, and comparing a result with an expected value treats every NaN as equal to every other NaN. Copying a NaN never changes it (VM-10.3).
`c` may be the same slot as `a` or `b`: both operands are read before `c` is written.

`ADD_V` and `SUB_V` compute `c[i] = a[i] + b[i]` (or `-`) for `i` = 0, 1, 2 in that order, each component as VM-4.1. Each component reads its operands after the previous component's result is written, so when `c` overlaps `a` or `b` shifted by one or two slots, later components see the values just written. The C writes the components in this order, but because the operands are then partially overlapping objects a compiler may reorder the reads (GCC at `-O2` does unless given `-fno-strict-aliasing`); this spec fixes the source order.

`MUL_V` is the dot product: `c = (a[0]*b[0] + a[1]*b[1]) + a[2]*b[2]`, three products and two sums, each rounded to f32 as VM-4.1, added left to right, with no fused multiply-add. All six inputs are read before the one result slot is written. id's x87 build kept the intermediate values at a higher precision and could differ in the last bit; this spec fixes per-operation f32 rounding, which every SSE and ARM build gives when compiled without contraction (`-ffp-contract=off`).
`MUL_FV` computes `c[i] = a * b[i]` for `i` = 0, 1, 2 in order, reading the float `a` again for each component, so when `c[0]` is `a`'s slot the later components use the new value.
`MUL_VF` computes `c[i] = b * a[i]` for `i` = 0, 1, 2 in order, reading the float `b` again for each component in the same way.
`EQ_F`, `NE_F`, `LE`, `GE`, `LT` and `GT` write `1.0` to `c` when `a == b`, `a != b`, `a <= b`, `a >= b`, `a < b` or `a > b` holds for the floats, and `0.0` when it does not.

The comparisons are IEEE 754's: `-0` equals `+0`, and a NaN is unordered with everything including itself, so `EQ_F`, `LE`, `GE`, `LT` and `GT` give `0.0` and `NE_F` gives `1.0` when either operand is a NaN.

`EQ_V` gives `1.0` when all three components are equal as VM-6.2 says, and `NE_V` gives `1.0` when any component is unequal; a NaN in any component makes `EQ_V` `0.0` and `NE_V` `1.0`, even comparing a vector with itself.
All inputs are read before `c` is written, so `c` may overlap `a` or `b`.
