`EQ_S` compares the two strings by content with `strcmp`: the bytes from each string value's offset up to its NUL (PROGS-11.1), compared as unsigned bytes. It writes `1.0` when they are equal. Different offsets holding the same text are equal, and offset 0 equals every empty string.

`NE_S` writes `strcmp`'s result converted to float: `0.0` when the strings are equal, otherwise the first differing byte of `a` minus that of `b`, both as unsigned bytes, the NUL at the end of the shorter string counting as 0. C fixes only the sign of `strcmp`; this spec fixes the byte difference, which glibc and macOS's C library return. Code that only tests the result for zero is unaffected.

A string value is an offset into the string table or a string the engine allocated (PROGS-11.6). `EQ_S`, `NE_S` and `NOT_S` resolve both: a value from 0 to `numstrings - 1` reads the string table (PROGS-11.1), and any other value reads the engine-allocated string it names (EDICT-13.1), id's `PR_GetString` computing `pr_strings + value` for either. Only a value that is neither a table offset nor an engine-allocated string names memory outside both, which is undefined in C; this spec fixes the answer: `EQ_S`, `NE_S` and `NOT_S` with such a value fail with a runtime error (VM-19.7).

`EQ_E` and `NE_E` compare the 32-bit patterns of `a` and `b`, and `EQ_FNC` and `NE_FNC` compare them as function indices, writing `1.0` or `0.0`. None of them checks that the value names an entity or function, and `EQ_E` compares bits, not floats: `-0.0` and `0.0` differ, and a NaN pattern equals itself.
`NOT_F` writes `1.0` when the float `a` equals `0.0` (so for `+0` and `-0`) and `0.0` otherwise, including for a NaN.
`NOT_V` writes `1.0` when all three components of `a` equal `0.0`.

`NOT_S` writes `1.0` when the string value is 0 or names an empty string (its first byte is NUL), and `0.0` otherwise. It resolves the value the same way `EQ_S` does (VM-7.3): a table offset reads the string table, and a value outside the table reads the engine-allocated string it names (PROGS-11.6, EDICT-13.1), so an engine-made string is false only when its text is empty (EDICT-13.2); a value that is neither fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7).
`NOT_ENT` writes `1.0` when the entity value is 0, the world, and `0.0` otherwise. It compares the value only, without checking that it names an edict or whether that edict is free.
`NOT_FNC` writes `1.0` when the function index is 0.
`AND` writes `1.0` when the floats `a` and `b` are both non-zero, and `OR` when either is. A NaN is non-zero and `-0` is zero. Both operands are always read; C's short-circuit has no visible effect.

These opcodes read their operands as floats, unlike `IF` and `IFNOT` (VM-13.3), which test the 32-bit pattern: a slot holding `-0.0` is false for `NOT_F`, `AND` and `OR` but true for `IF`. An integer value read as a float (a string offset, an entity value) is zero only when its pattern is 0x00000000 or 0x80000000.

`BITAND` and `BITOR` convert each float operand to a 32-bit signed integer by truncation toward zero, take the two's complement AND or OR, and write the integer converted back to float, rounded to nearest even, so a result above 2^24 can lose its low bits.

Converting a NaN, an infinity or a value whose truncation is outside -2^31 to 2^31 - 1 is undefined in C. This spec fixes the result of the conversion as -2147483648 (0x80000000), the value an x86 build produces: the "integer indefinite" result of SSE's `cvttss2si` and of the x87 `fist` instructions. An ARM build gives a different value (it saturates, and a NaN becomes 0), so an oracle run of these vectors is on x86.
Negative operands work in two's complement: `-8 | 3` is `-5` and `-1 & 5` is `5`.
`STORE_F`, `STORE_S`, `STORE_ENT`, `STORE_FLD` and `STORE_FNC` copy the 32-bit pattern of slot `a` to slot `b`. They are the same operation: the type in the name is not checked.

`STORE_V` copies slots `a`, `a+1`, `a+2` to `b`, `b+1`, `b+2` one at a time in that order. When `b` is `a+1` or `a+2` a later copy reads a slot already written, so `STORE_V 100 101` sets slots 101 to 103 to the old value of slot 100. This is the source order, fixed as in VM-5.1.

Every copy is bit-exact, including `-0.0` and every NaN pattern, signalling NaNs among them. `STORE_V` copies through float assignments in C, which id's x87 build may have done by loading and storing through the FPU, quietening a signalling NaN; this spec fixes the bit-exact copy, which no QC arithmetic can tell apart because no arithmetic produces a signalling NaN.
In a store, `b` is the destination and `c` is unused, unlike the other opcodes, which write their result to `c`.

`LOAD_F`, `LOAD_S`, `LOAD_ENT`, `LOAD_FLD` and `LOAD_FNC` take an entity value in `a` (PROGS-17.4) and a field index in `b` (PROGS-17.5), and copy the 32-bit pattern of that entity's field slot `b` to slot `c`. They are the same operation.
`LOAD_V` copies the entity's field slots `b`, `b+1`, `b+2` to `c`, `c+1`, `c+2`.
A load works on any edict: the world and free edicts are read like any other.

id does not check the entity value or the field index (`PARANOID` is off), so a value that does not name an edict, or a field slot outside `0` to `entityfields - 1`, reads other memory, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: such a load fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7). Which entity values name an edict is EDICT-1.9.

`ADDRESS` takes an entity value in `a` and a field index in `b` and writes to `c` a pointer to that entity's field slot `b` (PROGS-17.7). In id's engine the pointer is the entity value plus the byte offset of the fields within an edict plus `4 * b`; the offset is engine-specific (`edicts.md`), so only `STOREP` gives a pointer meaning.

`ADDRESS` on the world (entity value 0) fails with `assignment to world entity` while the server is active (`sv.state == ss_active`). While a map is loading (`ss_loading`, when spawn functions run) it succeeds.
`ADDRESS` reads no field and checks neither the field index nor whether the edict is free.

`STOREP_F`, `STOREP_S`, `STOREP_ENT`, `STOREP_FLD` and `STOREP_FNC` copy the 32-bit pattern of slot `a` to the field slot that the pointer in slot `b` names; `STOREP_V` copies slots `a` to `a+2` to that field slot and the next two, in order.

id writes wherever the pointer leads, which is undefined in C when it is not a field slot of an edict. This spec fixes the answer: a `STOREP` whose pointer does not name a field slot of an edict, or for `STOREP_V` three consecutive field slots of one edict, fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7) without writing.
`STOREP` does not check for the world or a free edict: a pointer to a world field made while loading still writes to the world when the server is active.
`GOTO` makes the next statement the current one plus `a`, a signed offset (PROGS-7.2).
`IF` makes the next statement the current one plus `b` when the 32-bit pattern in slot `a` is not zero, and the current one plus one otherwise. `IFNOT` jumps by `b` when the pattern is zero.
The test is on the 32-bit pattern, not on the float: `-0.0` (0x80000000) and every NaN are true, and a string value is true when its offset is not 0, even if the string it names is empty.
An offset of 0 jumps to the same statement, so `GOTO 0` repeats until the runaway guard stops it (VM-3.1).
A jump outside the statements table is VM-3.3's error.

`CALL0` to `CALL8` call the function whose index is in slot `a`. The call sets the argument count (`pr_argc`), which builtins read, to the number in the opcode name. The arguments are already in the parameter slots `OFS_PARM0` to `OFS_PARM7` (PROGS-18.1), written by earlier statements; the call itself moves nothing.
A function index of 0 fails with `NULL function`.
id reads `pr_functions[index]` without checking, so a negative index or one not less than `numfunctions` is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: it fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7).

When the function is a builtin (`first_statement` below 0, PROGS-10.2), its number is `-first_statement`; a number of `LIMIT_NUM_BUILTINS` or more fails with `Bad builtin call number` (LIMIT-5.1, LIMIT-5.3). Otherwise the builtin is called directly: no frame is pushed, the call depth does not change (LIMIT-2.3), no locals are saved and no parameters are copied. A builtin returns a value by writing `OFS_RETURN`. When it returns, execution continues with the statement after the call.
When the function is a QC function it is entered as VM-15 says, and execution continues at its `first_statement`. The statement after the call runs when it returns (VM-16.4).

The number in the opcode is not checked against the callee's `numparms`: the callee copies `numparms` parameters from the parameter slots whatever they hold, including values left there by earlier calls.

Entering pushes a frame holding the current statement and the current function, and adds one to the call depth; when the new depth is `LIMIT_MAX_STACK_DEPTH` or more it fails with `stack overflow` (LIMIT-2.1). The depth is checked before the local stack.

Next it saves the callee's `locals` slots, from `parm_start` up, onto the local stack above the slots in use. When the slots in use plus `locals` is more than `LIMIT_LOCALSTACK_SIZE` it fails with `PR_ExecuteProgram: locals stack overflow` before saving anything (LIMIT-3.1).

Then it copies the parameters: with `o` starting at `parm_start`, for each parameter `i` from 0 to `numparms - 1` and each `j` from 0 to `parm_size[i] - 1`, slot `4 + 3*i + j` is copied to slot `o` and `o` goes up by one. Parameters are packed: a float parameter after a vector parameter lands at `parm_start + 3`. The copy comes after the save, so the saved values are the caller's.

`parm_size` is not checked: a size above 3 reads on past the parameter's three slots into the next parameter's, and past slot 27 into ordinary globals. A `numparms` of 0 or less copies nothing (PROGS-10.5).
The callee becomes the current function and execution continues at its `first_statement`.

A negative `locals` makes id move the local stack's top down, and a later entry or return writes outside it, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer: entering a function whose `locals` is negative fails with a runtime error (VM-19.7). A save, restore or parameter copy that reaches a global slot outside the globals is VM-1.4's error.

Entering does not clear the local slots: a local that is not a parameter starts with whatever value its global slot held, normally the value left by the caller or by the last function that used the slot.

`DONE` and `RETURN` are the same operation. They copy slots `a`, `a+1`, `a+2` to `OFS_RETURN` (slots 1, 2, 3), one slot at a time in that order. All three are copied, even for a function returning a float or nothing.

qcc ends every function with `DONE 0 0 0`, so falling off the end copies slot 0 to slot 1, then slot 1 (now slot 0's value) to slot 2, then slot 2 to slot 3: all three return slots get slot 0's value, normally 0. A function that returns nothing therefore clears the return slots.

After the copy, the current function's `locals` slots are restored from the top of the local stack to `parm_start` up, the slots in use drop by `locals`, and the frame is popped: the current function and statement become the ones the frame saved. The return value is copied before the restore, so a function can return one of its own locals.

When the call depth is then back at the exit depth of the current run (VM-2.3), `PR_ExecuteProgram` returns to its caller. Otherwise execution continues with the statement after the call in the restored function.
The return copy is bit-exact, as VM-10.3 fixes for `STORE_V`.

`PR_LeaveFunction`'s own checks, `prog stack underflow` (through `Sys_Error`) and `PR_ExecuteProgram: locals stack underflow`, cannot fail: every return matches an entry of the same function, and `locals` is never negative (VM-15.6).

`STATE` acts on the entity in the global `self`. It sets that entity's `nextthink` field to the global `time` plus 0.1, added in double precision: `(float)((double)time + 0.1)`, where 0.1 is the double nearest to 0.1, not the float.

It sets the entity's `frame` field to the float in `a` only when that float is not equal to the current `frame` as VM-6.2 compares: when `a` is `-0.0` and `frame` is `+0.0`, or the reverse, `frame` keeps its bits, and when `a` is a NaN `frame` becomes that NaN.
It sets the entity's `think` field to the 32-bit pattern in `b`, a function index that is not checked.

`STATE` does not check for the world: with `self` 0 it writes the world's fields. A `self` that does not name an edict is VM-11.4's error. Where `self`, `time`, `nextthink`, `frame` and `think` are is in `edicts.md`; in id's `progdefs.q1` they are global slots 28 and 31 and field slots 46, 30 and 44.
A nested run shares the call stack, the call depth, the local stack and the globals with the outer run, and has its own runaway counter and exit depth (LIMIT-2.2, LIMIT-4.2).

When the nested run returns, the current function and statement are again the outer function and its call statement, restored from the frame the nested entry pushed; the builtin then returns and the outer run continues with the statement after the call.
A nested run clears the statement trace flag (VM-2.3), so tracing started before it is off after it.
An error in a nested run ends every run, not only the nested one (VM-19.2).

A runtime error from the VM (`stack overflow`, `PR_ExecuteProgram: locals stack overflow`, `runaway loop error`, `NULL function`, `Bad builtin call number`, `Bad opcode <op>`, `assignment to world entity`), like one from a builtin, goes through `PR_RunError`. It prints the current statement (the last one VM-3.1 made current, so for `runaway loop error` the statement before the one that was not run), then the call stack from the innermost function out as `<file> : <function>`, then the message; it sets the call depth to 0 ("dump the stack so host_error can shutdown functions") and calls `Host_Error ("Program error")`.
`Host_Error` ("This shuts down both the client and server") never returns: no further statement of any run executes, at any level of nesting, and `PR_ExecuteProgram` does not return to its caller.
**Withdrawn** 2026-10-20: it said the call depth is 0 after any error, but a host error that does not go through `PR_RunError` (VM-2.1, BUILTIN-3.2) leaves it; replaced by VM-19.6.
**Withdrawn** 2026-10-20: it gave VM-2.2 the effects of a runtime error, which resets the call depth, where VM-2.2 fails as VM-2.1 does, a host error that keeps it; replaced by VM-19.7.

An opcode that fails writes no global and no field. It may already have set the argument count (a failing call) or counted against `profile` (VM-3.4). A builtin that fails may have written before it failed (`builtins.md`).

After a runtime error the call depth is 0. After a host error that does not go through `PR_RunError`, `PR_ExecuteProgram: NULL function` (VM-2.1, VM-2.2) or a builtin's `error` or `objerror` (BUILTIN-3.2), it is still the depth at the error. Either way the local stack is not reset: the slots the aborted functions saved stay in use, are never restored and are never released, since nothing outside `pr_exec.c` touches `localstack_used`. The globals keep the values they had when the error happened, including the locals of the aborted functions.

The errors this spec adds where id's C is undefined (VM-1.4, VM-2.4, VM-3.3, VM-7.3, VM-11.4, VM-12.5, VM-14.3, VM-15.6) are runtime errors with the effects of VM-19.1, VM-19.2 and VM-19.6. id has no message for them, so the message is the implementation's. VM-2.2 is the host error of VM-2.1.
A WAD2 file starts with a 12-byte header: the four bytes `WAD2` (0x57 0x41 0x44 0x32), then `numlumps` and `infotableofs` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers.

If the first four bytes are not exactly `WAD2`, loading fails with the error `Wad file <name> doesn't have WAD2 id` (fatal in id's engine). `wad.h` comments the field "should be WAD2 or 2DAW", but the code accepts only `WAD2`; `WAD3` and `2DAW` fail.
A file of fewer than 12 bytes fails to load. id's code reads the header from the loaded buffer without checking its length, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
The engine finds `gfx.wad` through the game filesystem (FS-3), so a mod can replace it; if it is not found, the engine stops with the fatal error `W_LoadWadFile: couldn't load gfx.wad`.

The directory is `numlumps` 32-byte entries at offset `infotableofs`: `filepos`, `disksize` and `size` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers, then the `type` and `compression` bytes, two unused bytes and a 16-byte name.
`numlumps` 0 gives an archive with no lumps, which loads without error.

A negative `numlumps` fails to load. id's loop compares an unsigned counter with it, so it walks about four billion entries past the buffer, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

A directory that does not lie wholly inside the file (a negative `infotableofs`, or `infotableofs + 32 * numlumps` past the end) fails to load. id's code does not check it, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

Each lump name is cleaned when the archive loads (`W_CleanupName`): the bytes of the 16-byte field up to the first NUL are kept, ASCII `A` to `Z` become `a` to `z`, every other byte (including 0x80 to 0xFF) is unchanged, and the rest of the field is filled with NUL. The comment above `W_CleanupName` says it pads with spaces; the code pads with NUL. Bytes after the first NUL are discarded.
A 16-byte name field with no NUL keeps all 16 bytes as the name. id's `strcmp` on such a name reads past the field, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as a 16-byte name.

`type`, `compression` and `disksize` are not checked. The engine uses `type` only to byte-swap the width and height of `TYP_QPIC` (66) lumps, which changes nothing on little-endian hosts. `compression` is ignored: `CMP_LZSS` (1) is defined in `wad.h` but no WinQuake code decompresses a lump, so a lump's bytes are always returned as stored.
`filepos`, `disksize` and `size` are not checked when the archive loads, so a bad range never stops an archive from loading or its directory from being listed.
Lumps keep their directory order, and two lumps may have the same cleaned name.

A lookup cleans the requested name by the rule of WAD-2.5 and returns the first lump, in directory order, whose cleaned name equals it. Lookups therefore ignore ASCII case (`CoNcHaRs` finds `CONCHARS`) but not the case of bytes 0x80 to 0xFF.

Only the first 16 bytes of the requested name count. A requested name of 16 or more bytes is compared as its first 16 bytes; id's code compares an unterminated buffer there, which is undefined, and this spec fixes the answer by WAD-2.6.
A name that matches no lump is the error `W_GetLumpinfo: <name> not found` (fatal in id's engine).

A lump's data starts at `filepos`. QuakeC Studio reads a lump as the `disksize` bytes at `filepos` (the bytes stored in the file; the engine itself never needs a length), and reading a lump whose range does not lie wholly inside the file is an error. The lump is still listed (WAD-2.8).

Looking up a lump by index accepts 0 to `numlumps - 1`. id's `W_GetLumpNum` accepts `numlumps` too (its test is `num > wad_numlumps`), which reads one entry past the directory; this spec fixes `numlumps` as an error. `W_GetLumpNum` has no caller in WinQuake (GitHub code search of `id-Software/Quake`, 2026-10-16, finds it only in `wad.c` and `wad.h`).
A picture lump (`TYP_QPIC`) is a `width` and a `height`, signed 32-bit little-endian, followed by `width * height` bytes of palette indices, row by row from the top left.

The `conchars` lump has no header: it is 128 by 128 bytes of palette indices, 16 rows of 16 characters of 8 by 8 pixels, character `n` at row `n >> 4` and column `n & 15`, with index 0 drawn as transparent.

A texture lump (`TYP_MIPTEX`) starts with a `miptex_t`: a 16-byte name, then `width`, `height` and four mip offsets as unsigned 32-bit little-endian integers, the offsets from the start of the lump. id's engine never reads a texture lump from a WAD; the same structure in a BSP file is the BSP spec's, and WAD2 texture files are read only by map tools and editors.

A chunk is a 4-byte id, a signed 32-bit little-endian length, and that many bytes of data. The next chunk starts `8 + ((length + 1) & ~1)` bytes after the chunk's start: the data is padded to an even length.

Finding a chunk walks the chunks from a start offset to the end of the file and returns the first whose id equals the four bytes asked for, compared exactly (case matters). The lengths of enclosing chunks, including the `RIFF` chunk's, are not used: every search runs to the end of the file.
A search stops, finding nothing, at a chunk whose length is negative, or when the next chunk would start at or past the end of the file.

A search also stops, finding nothing, when fewer than 8 bytes are left for a chunk header. id's code reads the header past the end of the buffer, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as not found.

The next chunk's offset is computed without overflow: a length of 2147483647 puts the next chunk past the end of the file, so the search stops. In id's code `length + 1` overflows a signed integer there, which is undefined.

The file must contain a `RIFF` chunk, found by WAV-1 from the start of the file, whose bytes 8 to 11 are `WAVE`. Otherwise reading fails with the error `Missing RIFF/WAVE chunks`. The `RIFF` chunk need not be the first chunk in the file, and one that ends before byte 12 is missing.
Every later search starts 12 bytes after the start of the `RIFF` chunk.
A `fmt ` chunk must be found, or reading fails with the error `Missing fmt chunk`. Its format tag must be 1, or reading fails with the error `Microsoft PCM format only`.

`channels` is the signed 16-bit value at offset 10 of the `fmt ` chunk, `rate` the signed 32-bit value at 12 and `width` the signed 16-bit value at 22 divided by 8, with C integer division truncating toward zero (16 bits give 2, 12 give 1, 7 give 0). The `fmt ` chunk's own length is not checked: a short chunk's fields come from the bytes after it.
A `fmt ` field that lies past the end of the file fails reading with the error `Missing fmt chunk`. id's code reads past the buffer, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

If a `cue ` chunk is found, `loopstart` is the signed 32-bit value at offset 32 of it, the sample offset of the first cue point; the number of cue points and the chunk's length are not checked. With no `cue ` chunk, `loopstart` is -1. A value past the end of the file is read as if there were no `cue ` chunk (id's code reads past the buffer, which is undefined).

After a `cue ` chunk, a `LIST` chunk is searched for from the chunk after the `cue ` chunk. If one is found and its bytes 28 to 31 are `mark`, the loop's sample count `samples = loopstart + n`, where `n` is the signed 32-bit value at offset 24. Bytes 28 to 31 past the end of the file mean no `mark`.

A `data` chunk must be found, or reading fails with the error `Missing data chunk`. id's code prints the message and returns what it has read, so the engine then plays the bytes at the start of the file as samples; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
`width` 0 fails reading with the error `Sound <name> has a bad sample width`. id's code divides the `data` length by it, which on x86 stops the program with a divide error.

The `data` chunk's sample count is its length divided by `width`, truncating toward zero, and `dataofs` is 8 bytes after the start of the chunk. When WAV-2.7 gave a non-zero `samples`, the data's count must be at least that, or reading fails with the error `Sound <name> has a bad loop length` (fatal in id's engine); otherwise `samples` is the data's count.

A loop length from WAV-2.7 that is negative, or whose sum overflows a signed 32-bit integer, fails reading with the error `Sound <name> has a bad loop length`. id's code overflows a signed integer, which is undefined, or keeps a negative length the mixer cannot play; this spec fixes both as an error.

The `data` chunk's length is not checked against the file. `samples` counts what the chunk declares; a reader gets only the sample bytes that lie inside the file, and the samples after them are silence. id's code reads past the buffer there, which is undefined.
A sound plays only if `channels` is 1. Any other value, including the 0 a failed `GetWavinfo` leaves, makes the engine print `<name> is a stereo sample` and not load the sound (not fatal).

A sample is 8-bit unsigned with 128 as silence when `width` is 1, and 16-bit signed little-endian when `width` is 2. Any other `width` fails with the error `<name> has a bad sample width`: `ResampleSfx` reads any width but 2 as 8-bit samples while keeping the width as given, so id's engine has no single meaning for it, and this spec fixes the answer as an error.

`rate` must be greater than 0, or loading fails with the error `<name> has a bad sample rate`. id's code divides the sample count by `rate` divided by the output rate and converts the result to an integer, which for 0 or less is undefined or a negative allocation; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
`loopstart` -1 means the sound does not loop; any other value is the sample the sound loops back to, and is not checked against `samples`.

`S_LoadSound` loads the sound named `<name>` (the name `precache_sound` and `sound` give) from the file `sound/<name>` only: `Q_strcpy(namebuffer, "sound/");` then `Q_strcat(namebuffer, s->name);`, and `COM_LoadStackFile(namebuffer, ...)`. A `.wav` file anywhere else on the search path is never loaded as a sound, so the checks of WAV-3.1 to WAV-3.4 say nothing about it. The 2021 rerelease ships such files, its DualSense haptics clips under `tactile/dualsense/` (stereo, which WAV-3.1 would reject), read only by its own engine.
